Brahmā said:
Thus, those two, Vajra and Kāla, endowed with strength and possessing great power,
questioned the king of planets, Bhārgava, the delighter of the Bhrigus.
O Blessed One, sent by him from our side regarding the Vinaya,
we have gone to the various directions and regions throughout the earth with its seven continents.
Having conquered the seven netherworlds and brought their inhabitants under control,
they have established kings in your governance and have come here to your side.

Chapter Four The Fourth Chapter, transcribed with the suggested modifications (19.11.2019).
Brahmā said:
Thus, those two, Vajra and Kāla, endowed with strength and possessed of great power,
questioned Bhārgava, the descendant of Bhṛgu, the king of the planets.
O Blessed One, sent by our father for the sake of the Vinaya,
we have gone to all directions, to various lands, and throughout the earth with its seven islands.
[004:002] [Vijayaṃ ka ga]
Having conquered the seven netherworlds and brought their subjects under control,
they have established kings in your governance and have come here to your side.
"By what means shall we conquer Indra and the others and win heaven?
Tell me this very thing, O you who have exerted yourself in all branches of knowledge.
Śukra said:

The entire Jambūdvīpa, the earth with its seven continents, and even the netherworlds (pātālas) are easily attained; however, heaven is achieved only with great difficulty. Therein dwells Hari, the Lord of Gods, who is praised by all the deities.
Viṣṇu is the god who is the soul of all; Brahmā is the one proficient in the Vedas;
and Bṛhaspati is the one of great wisdom who has exerted himself in the science of polity (Arthaśāstra).
Indra, as well as Mahābala, Dhanada, Vahni, Nirṛti, Marut, Vāyu, Yama, wherever the moon and sun may be,
the Viśvedevas, Vasus, Rudras, the planets, the lunar mansions, and the stars;
He went to Marudvṛdhā.
O Kāla, heaven, which is protected by Dharma, cannot be conquered;
enjoy the royal realms and the netherworlds through the instruction of the duties of kingship.
Otherwise, a kingdom obtained in accordance with dharma surely goes to ruin,
like a battle between a cat and a mouse, or like that between a crow and an owl.
Just as a buffalo against a horse, or an elephant against the king of beasts,
so too is this battle with you gods called a "single-limbed" conflict;
for [the enemy] does not know the enjoyment of battle, nor the time, nor the place.
[004:011] [In a variant reading of the Kha manuscript, it is stated: "Only the battle is mentioned"; in the Ka and Ga manuscripts, it is "the section on the battle.
Furthermore, in a variant reading of the Kha manuscript, it says: "They were likewise unaware of the time and the place."]
Those kings who fight against the strength of our enemy forces go to their own destruction, for they are averse to statesmanship.
For in battle, strategy is powerful when accompanied by divine fortune;
likewise, those kings who fight after having understood the nature of human effort attain victory and the destruction of their enemies without hesitation.
The earth, together with its excellent cities, mountains, forests, and groves,
remains stable for as long as life lasts for those whose policy is hereditary;
having obtained the kingdom through righteousness, their victory shall likewise arise from righteousness alone.
[Not by sequence... nor by dharma, nor by sacrifice to the gods...
And as for the gods—Rudra, Brahmā, Indra, Keśava, Ravi, and Candramas—whoever among them one should wish to fight, how could that person be happy? [004:016]
Who among these would desire wealth? Who among these would not desire their destruction? For the gods never succeed against their enemies without war.
In battle, O child, there will be slaughter and the destruction of one's circle of kinsmen;
wealth perishes in war, as do horses, elephants, and those of great strength—
even when the field is level, it becomes treacherous where Śaṅkara and Keśava are present.
Kāla said:
"The great serpents, beginning with Ananta, are most terrible, possessing the venom of their very glance."
The Asuras and Rākṣasas dwelling in the depths of Pātāla have been conquered; indeed,
they cannot be defeated even by the high-souled Śaṅkara,
let alone by the wretched king of the gods or by a mere Brahmin.
Who would be capable in battle against me, whose companion is Vajradaṇḍa, and who holds a sword in hand— once I have been dragged by the noose of Time? [004:021]
Whether it be Brahmā or Rudra, who is saluted by all the gods—
the earth has been conquered by us, as well as the realm of Pātāla and its serpents.
When, upon merely seeing his master, one has attained heaven,
then victory shall likewise bring fame, while defeat brings the supreme goal for one who has begun [the undertaking].
"O tiger among the planets, we have set out; you should grant us your permission. Having thus taken leave of Śukra in the month of Nabhas, [or rather, in the month of Uttarāṣāḍhā].
Then, when the moon was in the constellation Uttarāṣāḍhā on the second lunar day,
they both set out; having gone to the Nandana grove with their entire army, they remained there.
Yamāntaka is in the eastern direction on Meru, while Ghora is in the north;
Vajradaṇḍa is in the west, and Kāla himself is in the south.
Having thus encircled it with a thousand million times ten million folds,
they ascended the city of Yama, which is situated above Mount Meru.
[He ascended the city of Yama.]
There, they beheld the daughter of Vivasvat, possessed of many moats and exceedingly radiant;
and there Yama, mounted upon his buffalo, with a terrible black face and great strength, stood with a staff in hand and his noose of Time raised aloft.
And Yama ascended his chariot;
then that army of Dānavas, while fighting in the great battle,
was shattered by the high-souled King Yama with his own forces.
Seeing her suddenly broken, Hālāhala— blazing with rage,
O Śakra, and possessed of great strength and prowess—
stood up and [struck] with a sharp axe that shone like ten thousand suns.
Desiring to slay the army born of Yama as an elephant destroys a lotus pond,
the powerful Yamāntaka likewise created a force consisting of great illusions;
he manifested a buffalo of immense strength to bring about the defeat of the buffalo-demon of Yama.
When Time and the End-maker had struck him down with his staff,
he became one-fold, ten-fold, hundred-fold,
and even thousand-fold.
The master of illusion indeed created tens of thousands, hundreds of thousands, and millions;
seeing them, Dharmarāja perceived himself surrounded a hundredfold.
Abandoning his mounts and weapons, he went to the city of Agni;
for the terrible enemy, having seen that army, found it difficult to look upon—
[the all-pervading lord was difficult to behold].
Mounted upon the goat, they all engaged in battle with that fire,
which, with its hundreds of thousands of flames, rose up like the fire of cosmic destruction (Kālānala).
[The fire, by the discharge of its flames...]
Śakra suddenly incinerated the army of Vajradaṇḍa;
his city, Tejovatī, with its copper walls and archways,
was likewise consumed.

Likewise, brahmins with sacrificial ladles (*sruc*) in their hands arose by the hundreds of thousands; through meditation, they incinerated the entire army born of the formidable Vibhu. [004:038] [With sacrificial ladles in hand...]
Having seen it thus, Time (Kāla) should likewise pacify it with the water arising from the illusion of clouds by means of the all-pervading Staff-bearer (Daṇḍin).

One should cause all cruel things to sprout forth by means of those who offer the nectar of the mind; thus is that splendor arising from the fire of anger pacified. [If one whose senses are sated by the taste of the nectar of the mind causes all cruel things to sprout forth...]
It rained mud, moss, plantains, and blue lotuses.
Having thus seen his own army defeated by the staff, Pāvaka abandoned his pride in his splendor and departed for Indra’s Amarāvatī.
Seeing Yama and Agni approaching together with Indra,
he was seized by great agitation and mounted his lordly elephant.
Resembling Mount Udayācala, with a body as red as vermilion,
rich with the sound of bells and tinkling ornaments, adorned with chowries,
a great elephant with four tusks that strikes fear into the enemies of the gods.
The mighty wielder of the thunderbolt, the lord of the gods, ascended,
placing Mātali in front, as did the Viśvedevas and others.
The Vaiṣṇavas, Vāruṇas, Saumyas, Aindras, and likewise the Cāndras;
Kubera, Dhanada, Candra, Vāyu, and Varuṇa—
these were the warriors.
Having heard of the battle of the Lord of the Gods, all the Bhallāṭas, desiring to fight there,
arrived in a mere moment with their own weapons raised in their hands.
Thus, O Śakra, when those thirty gods, together with Śakra,
heard that they were eager for battle, the Lord himself, whose banner is Garuḍa, arrived there.
Indra, O supreme god, beheld him bearing the conch, the discus, and the mace.
Having seen him, he fell at his feet and worshipped with devotion through a hymn of praise.
Indra said:
Salutations to you, O Lord of the gods of gods, O Lord composed of all the gods!
You who hold the conch, discus, and mace in your hands, adorned with a garland of forest flowers,
O Lord of all the gods!
O you who bear the Śrīvatsa mark, O great-bodied one, adorned with the Kaustubha jewel upon your chest;
O destroyer of the enemies of the gods, O Lord of Devas, O you whose womb is the Vedas, salutations be to you!
You are the embodiment of the gods and yet formless, the bestower of the fruits of Vedic sacrifice.
O God, you who possess three forms and three courses, the destroyer of the fear of your devotees;
O embodiment of the Vedas, you who are equal toward friends, enemies, and those who are neutral, and the destroyer of the lineages of the wicked.

Save me, O Lord of the gods of gods, O yellow-robed one, Lord of the universe! O you who are impartial toward friend, enemy, and neutral alike, O vanquisher of the enemies of the gods— the deities, oppressed by the Dānavas, have come to you alone for refuge.
"The Lord of the Sacrifice (Yama) has been conquered, and Agni is endowed with blazing splendor.
Thus have you arrived, O Blessed One; what shall I do? Please command me.
Hearing these words spoken by Śakra, Viṣṇu, out of compassion, [replied].
The Lord, smiling, said: "Do not fear in my presence,
even though you are the Lord of the gods of gods, who took half of Umā’s body as your own."
O Lord of Gods, although he has arrived, let the enemy nevertheless be slain;
however, listen as I explain the underlying reason for this.
[004:057] [Let him be spared, O Kha.]
Viṣṇu said: There was once a preeminent lord of the asuras named Dundubhi;
by him, all the gods were defeated through the power of a boon from Brahmā.
Invincible even to Brahmā, Sūrya, Yama, and ourselves as well, he,
having then utterly defeated the gods, indeed caused them to fall from heaven.
At that time, O mighty-armed one, his lord became Śailaṅgama;
then he beheld the Goddess of the gods residing within the body of Śaṅkara.
Seeing her, his mind overwhelmed by passion, he became agitated and prepared to speak to the goddess; however, he was observed by the God. [The goddess was observed as he prepared to seize her.]
Then, suddenly consumed by the fire born from the eye of the God of gods through his wrath, that cruel Dānava— along with his weapons, chariot, foot-soldiers, and mounts— was reduced to ashes.
Seeing that [being] suddenly reduced to ashes, the three-eyed god [beheld it];
from those ashes, smoke-colored and indeed dark-red, yellow, black, and dark-green [vapors arose].
Having taken up white ashes, he shook the Goddess as well;
and by the striking of his hands against the ashes, there arose from the tips of his fingers a shower of ash that reached to the very end of the horizon.
A great wick was raised, adorned with all colors [variant:
raised, adorned with all threads];
beholding Umā, who is honored by the gods, shining brightly, a shadow endowed with all auspicious marks arose from her.
Then Umā, who is honored by the gods, being of great power and requesting a second portion of the deity,
remembered that terrible great Asura and uttered a curse.
"Go, O evil one of wicked conduct, to the surface of the earth, you who possess great strength!
There you shall become a terrible being, with a luster like that of a dark blue cloud."
Having assumed a massive form and struck fear into the gods, asuras, and rākṣasas,
the Lord then beheld him and said, "What is this that you have done?"
But who could grant him that?
For he is our conquered enemy, intent upon our destruction.
It is never appropriate to ever allow for the growth of an enemy's side.
And that fool who, out of joy, has treated the causal substances with partiality, shall go to his destruction through his own compassion for them.
Having uprooted everything completely except for a small remnant, yet leaving its root unexcavated,
that very thing becomes powerful once more and flourishes like the jujube tree.
Just as a tree laden with fruit is struck down by a storm,
so too have you, O evil-minded one, been brought low by me—
you who were an obstacle to the gods and a terror to sages and brahmins.

"It is not fitting for you, O dull-witted child, to always behave with the nature of a woman by increasing the host of enemies of the twice-born gods. Having been addressed thus by Śambhu, the Goddess looked at him in anger.
Having become supremely devoted to me, he will conquer all the gods;
for upon seeing her,
this supreme state of Viṣṇu will arise, and he shall be invincible.
A resident of the city of Kuśadvīpa, he will become Candraśobha, devoted to the state of Viṣṇu; he will take delight in the splendor of the worship in the city of Kuśadvīpa.
The seven islands, along with the netherworlds (pātāla), the seven worlds, and including Indra (vāsava)—all these shall belong to him.
"By becoming obedient to this, he shall become invincible.
Having heard these words of the goddess, which were spoken while she was on a path of error, Śiva, overcome with rage, cursed her: "And you shall go to the mortal world."
And there this man of evil conduct will beg for his fall;
thus, inflamed by the fire of anger, she shall curse the lord of the asuras.
Resembling a dark blue cloud in form, like another buffalo of Yama,
I, standing firm as a lioness, shall slay you while playing;
[blazing with the fire of my wrath].
The goddess spoke in anger, and the god likewise spoke to her:
"O Lord of the Gods, in this manner it was previously fashioned by Śambhu out of adamant (vajra).
[Thus she was provoked to anger.]
Having been born from the body of Dundubhi, he was devoted to me,
a resident of Candraśobhāpura, and ever intent upon my worship.
[sadejyakaḥ ka ga]
This teaching of his has been obtained, which is difficult even for Brahmins to endure;
how much more so for a Dānava who possesses all power? If that one of terrible name should come, he would destroy even Rudra and the others, despite their every effort.
Having heard that and having heard it thus from Hari, Brahmā said: "O Lord, tell me, what shall I do?
You have granted me heaven, and all my sacrifices have been protected."
Having heard this, [Ka-Ga; performing sacrifices, protected by Ka-Ga], you are the lord and master of the Indras, and you are the protector of the gods.
When this was said, Viṣṇu spoke: "Listen, Śakra, with a concentrated mind."
Then the highly intelligent Bṛhaspati, the Lord of Speech, arrived there;
having been thus addressed, Bṛhaspati spoke.
By the mere command of whom all the gods, together with the sun,
were subdued along with their power, like fire by water.
Who is capable of overthrowing him in battle while he is still possessed of his army—
be it Brahmā or even Rudra— if they are devoid of conciliation and statesmanship?
"O Lord, this which was given by you in the past— this invincibility against all the gods and that which was granted by Umā— is the thorn in the side of all the enemies of the gods."
O Lord, she was a knower of all the weapons and the principles, devoted to all dharmas,
and likewise devoted to you; her husband was devoted to her, and she was a devoted wife [devoted to you].
The protector of the world and protector of his subjects, established on the path of Dharma;
likewise, many kings, endowed with millions upon millions of virtues.
He possessed four times as many rutting elephants and horses as he did [other mounts];
all were equal to Airāvata, like mountains together with their foothills.
The Nārāyaṇa weapon, the Brahmā weapon, those of Śiva, or even those of Varuṇa—
by whom could the destruction of such an enemy as he be accomplished?
Even the sequence of place and time speaks only of a single means.

[The weapons of Nārāyaṇa, Brahmā, Śiva, and others... Furthermore, he who knows the seven [breaths], beginning with *ekā*, which are freed from the defects born of fear as well as those born of anger— he is a possessor of qualities (*guṇin*), the best among the qualified.
O Lord, just as pearls, elephants, horses, buffaloes, cats, mice, crows,
and owls are not for one's welfare when engaged in battle, so too is it with serpents against mongooses.
[Like a mouse and a crow...
Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Words of Bṛhaspati," in the *Śrī Devīpurāṇa* (within the *Brahmopadeśa*).
[Thus in the first *Devīpurāṇa*, Ka.]

The Fifth Chapter. The Blessed One said:
"It is indeed true, O highly wise Bṛhaspati, Lord of Speech."
You alone are worthy to know this, for you are the discernor of all principles of logic.
Who is capable of composing [this work], he who understands the systems of the *Śambhugītā*, the *Auśanasa*, his own [treatises],
and my own *Brahmagītās*— he alone is a master of speech.
O Lord of Speech,
where have you gone? With you as his protector and high-souled minister,
who here— even the wielder of the trident himself— would not be capable of being subdued?
Those six qualities, which are the foremost of all virtues and difficult to be understood even by great-souled ones, are indeed [the focus] for yogis and for ministers who discourse on treaties.
[The passage for the Sandhivādins is missing from the three manuscripts.
At the junctions of the joints, they are distinct, and the afflictions are equal in their defects.
But those two excellent physicians, being equal in power, maintained him for a long time.

[Where are the diseases? Where is equal splendor? O best of beings, you who know the way of the three times and are proficient in all branches of knowledge, tell this king of the gods what would be appropriate.
"Indeed, who are you?
Bṛhaspati said:
"O God of gods, O Sovereign of the Suras, O Wielder of the conch, discus, and mace!"
O destroyer of the Asuras, my auspicious mind is devoted to you, not to myself.
O Lord of Gods, our own power is evident before your very eyes,
in that we speak thus to the Great-Souled One as boldly as a woman of noble family might.
O Great-Souled One,
words imbued with virtue have issued forth from my mouth;
nevertheless, O Lord of Gods, tell me something concerning what is beneficial and what is harmful, O Master.
Having become obedient to his command, the denizens of heaven desire happiness;
let them abide by his word until the three-eyed God [Śiva].
Having thus deliberated, Śakra, Viṣṇu, and Bṛhaspati gratified the goddess Jayā, who dwells upon the Vindhya mountain.
They dispatched Nārada to issue the command of Vajradaṇḍa.
Viṣṇu said:
"O celestial sage, O lord of Brahmins, O son of Brahmā, O you of great asceticism!"
Go and speak to that wicked one, the son of Ghora, the enemy of the gods.
At Viṣṇu’s command, Nārada went to where that asura was;
seeing the Ṛṣi approaching, Kāla and Vajra honored him.
Nārada said: O Vajra, you are the fierce son of Ka, possessing great strength equal to that of Kāla.
The gods are well-established in the teaching, and your goddess is even more beloved to you.
How much more so for one who performs hundreds of sacrifices, or one devoted to Brahmā or Viṣṇu?
Enjoy heaven and the earth as long as the two gods, the destroyers of your enemies, endure.

Having performed a hundred sacrifices for Brahmā and sixty for Indra and Agni, Bṛhaspati and Viṣṇu went to heaven, where the god’s terrible command was issued, to the place where the Grandfather resided.
[Devādyā-ka] (Thus, in the Śrī Devīpurāṇa, in the section on the Incarnation of the Goddess, the fifth chapter, titled "The Arrival of Hari and Bṛhaspati at the Abode of Brahmā," [ends].)
[Thus ends the first incarnation of the Goddess, comprising her arrival at the abode of Brahmā and the dialogue between Hari and Bṛhaspati.]

Brahmā said:
Salutations to you, O Lord of universal form; salutations be to you, O source of the universe!
O glorious Vāsudeva, who embodies all the gods, salutations be to you!
O Lord of the Viśvedevas,
salutations to You, the cause and non-cause of the past, present,
and future; You who are without beginning, and the supreme cause of the beginning, middle, and end.
Obeisance to you, who exist as the future form and the form of the fish.
O Upholder of the Earth, Lord of the Tortoise, Varāha, King Narasiṃha;
O Lord of all Vedas, the one to be known, the end of the Vedāntas—salutations, salutations!
O Lord of all gods, homage be to you!
Homage to you, the Dwarf (Vāmana); O Rāma, Rāma, salutations again and again!
O Vāsudeva, homage to you; O God Kṛṣṇa, salutations again and again!
O Rāmadeva,
O you who have arisen from the body of the pure Buddha, whose nature is pure existence,
who are liberated from passion and hatred— homage be to you, wearer of the red robe! 006:005.

O red-robed one, mounted upon a horse, O mighty-armed one, you who set in motion the dharma of the Kali age; O God clad in the directions as your garment, you who set in motion the dharma of the Śūdras.
O destroyer of the tribes of Mlecchas, salutations to you in the form of Kalki; O initiator of the end of the age, the origin of the age, and the dharma of the age!
O you whose body is like Kapila,
salutations to you, O Lord of the gods of gods! O bestower of desired objects,
O God, may that which I wish for from you come to pass exactly so.
"O Keśava, O best of gods, in my affairs— both those tasks already desired and those things yet to come— please grant me your assistance."
Then, O Lord of the Gods, Viṣṇu was formerly pleased with me;
he became a granter of boons according to my desire and offered his assistance in whatever I wished for.
Thus, for one who contemplates this Vaiṣṇava hymn upon rising in the morning, at midday, and at the time of twilight, their every wish shall grant the fulfillment of desires.
[From here until the end of the chapter—the reading is simply "Viṣṇu-stava"]—One who desires a son obtains a son; one who desires wealth obtains wealth;
one who desires knowledge obtains knowledge; and one who desires happiness shall become a partaker of happiness.
Thus ends the hymn to Viṣṇu in the *Śrī Devīpurāṇa*, within the section on the descent of the Goddess.
[In manuscript G, it reads simply "Viṣṇustavaḥ"].
Brahmā said:
O God Janārdana, I and others previously told you:
"O Madhusūdana, the most excellent boon among the Asuras must not be granted."
As before,
the Asuras, having obtained boons and being excessive in their pride,
become harassers of the gods and destroyers of the twice-born and their sacrifices.
Nevertheless, O mighty-armed one! For the destruction of the Asura, let Govinda and Bṛhaspati, the lord of speech, be considered, O Brahmin.
[Brahmā and Govinda said: Brahmā spoke:
"O best of gods, although you alone are the knower of all things, nevertheless—"
However, that which arises from the requirements of the task must be spoken; there is no fault in this for Trivikrama.
O Puruṣottama, that which occurred in a former kalpa during the Bhautya Manvantara, O Hari,
was he who is the God of gods, Mahādeva, the supreme cause.
But in the north is heaven, all-pervading, without beginning or end, and auspicious;
for the sake of His will, the Lord of the gods stands there as the protector and sovereign.
[Who are the subjects? He who, though enraged, is not inflamed by anger; he who, established in austerity, protects the subjects. (In the Ga manuscript)
The son of Kālāgnirudra was born upon the Rudrapāṣāṇa rock;
there, the one of great strength and prowess named Hālāhala appeared.
"Where has he gone? Where is Vajrapāṣāṇa?
Having seen that terrible son of his, who was like a second fire, struck down by you with a mallet at that time, O Lord... [he has gone where?]"
Then that fire, awakened and inflamed by pure wrath,
emitted flames born of its own breath toward the ten directions.
At that time, you were possessed by delusion, and then a doubt arose in me; I then meditated upon Rudra, who holds the khaṭvāṅga staff and is like the sun.
That great and radiant Ka-ga, the very essence of the instrument that bestows the boon of meditative perfection,
dispatched Cāmuṇḍā, whose splendor was equal to the fire of cosmic destruction.
For your protection and for the quelling of our fire,
by the mere sight of her, that flame was extinguished.
Then, O Lord, that Hālāhala fire spoke to him with a roar:
"O Viṣṇu, let the reason be told why I have been struck by you."
And being entreated by you, O Lord, he went toward that fire;
"The time for the dissolution of Brahmā is complete, and the purifier [fire] is ready for me."

when the entire terrible force born of illusion, which was of a ruinous nature, had been warded off.

Between the slaying of Mahiṣa and the decapitation [of the demon], he was seen with a weapon in his fierce hand, threatening [his foes],
struck on the head, and entwined by a serpent-noose.
O Purandara, the goddess, when worshipped, slays the enemy;
O Śakra, she is established and honored by one who remembers her or even recites her mantra.
O Vāsava, a man who worships [the deity] bestows auspicious desires that are cherished by the mind;
whether the image be made of clay, stone, wood, or even earthenware.
On the full moon day of the month of Paṅkeṣṭa,
having fasted, being pure, having bathed, and being free from desire and anger; having abandoned all attachments, being joyful, with his mind fixed on that [deity], and permeated by that disposition.
Having offered flowers, perfumes, and oblations many times with various sacrificial foods,
one should offer sesame seeds, ghee, and barley, all consecrated with the *sarvamaṅgala* mantra.

thereafter, one should cause the consecration to be performed by those who have mastered that scripture.

Agastya said:
Having thus heard from the Grandfather (Brahmā) the yoga of action regarding the king of the gods,
he again asked for the hymn sung by Śambhu as it was in the past.
Śakra said:
"O Grandfather, tell me that hymn to the Goddess which was formerly spoken by Śambhu to Bhārgava, who was desirous of spiritual perfection."
Brahmā said: O Śakra, in former times, Śukra performed a most difficult penance for a thousand divine years on Kailāsa, the highest of peaks.
Nevertheless, the boon-granting destroyer of Tripura became exceedingly difficult for us to cross;
then the attendant Puṣpadanta, with a sweet voice, uttered this hymn of praise.
Having understood that [state] and having focused his mind upon it, Śukra, the son of Bhṛgu and the best among those who know the Vedas,
gratified the Lord of Gods with this hymn.
Śambhu [composed this] with a variegated arrangement of words, both graceful and sweet. ||033:005ef||
Śukra said:
One who knows Śakra, with palms joined in reverence and purified by devotion toward Śiva,
should petition Śaṅkara on behalf of those whose minds are distressed and terrified by the fear of worldly existence.
Behold this body, which is full of constant disease, shrouded in toil and suffering;
it is hungry and thirsty, terrifying to behold, and afflicted by shameless desire.

Seeing that those dwelling within the body are deceived, deprived of the path to liberation, and inflamed by the fire of anger—Śukra spoke this hymn of worship before Maheśvara: [The wicked conduct of those dwelling in the body, the waves of craving, and being devoid of the path to liberation, all ignited by the fire of wrath. Śukra spoke this hymn of worship before Maheśvara.
From this saṃsāra— which is fraught with manifold great terrors and intense sorrow,
and which is tightly constrained by the bonds of karma— a living being revolves like a water-wheel.
Having seen that this human condition, once attained, is like a bubble on restless water,
I have not honored anyone else with a different mind out of delusion, for everything is pervaded by the All-pervading One.
Blessed are those men on earth who have been summoned by you; they are doers of good, they are of virtuous nature, and they are patient.
Their birth has achieved its purpose, and they do not become objects of grief when they die here.
Those Śaṃlikas have,
in truth, taken refuge with the god Paśupati with their whole being;
yet that primary fruit desired by their hearts has not been attained by those eminent men.

Having approached that which is eternally worshipped with reverence by Brahmā, Upendra, the Maruts, Mahendra, the Vasus, and the Vidyādharas, as well as by hosts of sages and others such as the Daityas—[that Liṅga]. (033:009e-h) [Eternally worshipped].
(sadārcite ka)
Who would not worship that supreme god Paśupati, the cause of all causes, by whose forms as the universal self this entire world of moving and non-moving beings is pervaded? (3.10)
Sovereignty over the three worlds, as well as immortality, daughters of the lords of serpents, celestial women,
and these and other things— these are obtained by those with whom Hara became well-disposed.
Those whose bodies possess the splendor of majesty throughout the worlds, who bestow the goals of dharma, artha, and kāma,
and who illuminate their cheeks with the radiance of jeweled earrings;
They illuminate the quarters with the rays of their own beautiful luster, dispelling the darkness;
having thus propitiated all those various [deities], the gods attained supreme sovereignty. (33.12)
Having drunk at night the honey fragrant with the scent of blue lotus petals,
he enjoyed at will the beautiful, graceful, and charming embrace of true love.

[Yaśī ka; Nīlā ka; Vināsinī ka] Those virtuous ones who, having abandoned their human bodies, attained the state of Vidyādharas—was that because they had abandoned you, O Enemy of Kāma, or because the fruit of their eternal merit has departed from them? ||033:013e-h||
[Even with only one man, O Mātanga,] chariots with renowned warriors in battle [proceed] by way of elephants and horses;
and also with rutting elephants, exuding ichor from intoxication, their temples moist with temporal secretions.

Those standing at the gateway,
filled with joy, together with kings under raised white parasols, crush him with powder;

He who crushes the armies of his enemies with thousands of sharp swords, and before whom kings shine while obstructing all efforts for their own welfare; he who,

with his excellent horses, makes the directions of the sky turbid with the darkness of dust raised by those steeds whose faces are washed with the water of rut, whose eyes are dark and languid, and who are adorned with fine trappings— by whose sovereign power one travels with ease upon preeminent elephants and horses.
That which is proclaimed by those distinguished by their auspicious qualities, beginning with the *lagna* (the ascendant).

The betel leaf offered to Brahmins along with the three myrobalans and mango sprouts—take that away from their minds; for devotion to liberation stands firm through prostrating at the feet of the Sādhya.
Women whose eyes are like the delicate petals of the blooming calyx of a blue lotus, and whose silken garments cling to their waists, girdles, anklets, and thighs; 033:016a-d.

O King, that which is beloved by the gods, bound with vermilion, perfumed with honey, and surrounded by a multitude of serpents—
that is the white parasol with its golden staff.
Whether it be the dust raised by the hooves of Siddhas’ horses,
or the beautiful, waving fly-whisks that are flickering—
that is all [attained] by the man who bows at the feet of the Lord.
Those kings who were constantly being sung of by women intoxicated with passion, accompanied by the sounds of lutes, flutes, drums, and cymbals joined together in harmony; ||033:018a-d||
Dwelling upon that most excellent palace, white as a conch shell, the moon, or crystal,
those for whom Śiva is pleased rejoice for a long time like the inhabitants of heaven.

That which is radiant with the moonlight of the teeth from the lotus-face of my beloved, and flickering like a horse agitated by the fragrance of her breath, is made tremulous by her swaying. (033:019a-d)
Honey with the hue of the bandhūka flower, poured according to ritual into jeweled vessels and scented with blue lotuses,
is drunk out of devotion to the Teacher of the Gods.

Those whose silk garments cling to their full hips due to the soft tinkling of their girdles, whose eyes extend to the tips of their ears, who possess beautiful faces, and who have found their abode in loveliness; ||033:020a-d||
That women have come under the servitude of kings and their desires are subject to them—
this entire world is the fruit for those kings whose minds are purified by devotion to Śiva.
Those who slept at night upon beautiful couches within excellent palaces, and were incessantly embraced with longing by women overwhelmed by intoxication; |||033:021a-d||
Those who here attain the destruction of sleep through sweet sounds of song and musical instruments—
all that is the fruit of Śambhu’s favor, bestowed according to rule upon one who has properly accumulated merit.
Having shattered that [palace], which was constructed with thousands of various mechanical devices and filled with terrifying obstacles,
they enter the beautiful and pure inner apartments of the Daitya women.

Having shattered that [bondage], what is accomplished? An elixir of life (*rasāyana*), youthful women, and desires following after desire—all this becomes easily attainable for the wise through the grace of the Enemy of Desire (Śiva). ||033:022e-h||
All those noble men who have come for refuge, having abandoned other activities,
are devoted to worship, recitation, and fire-offerings at the three times of day, and are thus freed from diseases and other afflictions.
Having experienced all those various enjoyments, in time, through the exhaustion of their karma,
they are born upon the surface of the earth as rulers of the land, endowed with wealth and sovereignty.

Those fools who do not take refuge in Śambhu— the supreme cause, the bestower of boons, the god who cuts through the suffering of saṃsāra, and who is saluted by all the gods and asuras— [fall into ruin].
At the end of their causes,

those people in the world who are intent on satisfying themselves with the alms of others are born on earth as wretched men, always suffering, poorly clothed, and abandoned by virtue, wealth, and pleasure.
To him who is the sovereign of the world, the teacher of gods and asuras, worshipped by Brahmā and Indra;
who is established through the Vedas, their branches, and the six ancillaries, and conceived by the followers of Sāṃkhya and other systems.
Those who have cultivated their minds with their whole being toward the omniscient Lord, the Sovereign, the Three-eyed One,
shall never again behold the face of Yama, which is as dense with darkness as a blemish.
But those others who, desiring merit, rise every day with devotion and [worship] with well-prepared camphor, agallochum, and sandalwood, as well as with garlands and ornaments; ||033:026a-d||
By performing the worship of Śarva according to the prescribed rites with ablutions of milk and other substances,
the wise, having experienced all worldly enjoyments, go to the divine state.
Whatever dull-witted, ignorant, and deceitful people, following evil paths,
out of delusion revile the Lord— Śiva, who is peaceful, unborn, the primordial Puruṣa; [may they suffer].

Generosity, compassion for living beings, following the instructions of the guru, patience, and freedom from attachment;

Those by whom wealth was not given to worthy recipients or to the destitute according to their means; by whom knowledge was not acquired; by whom fame was not spread; and by whom virtue was not preserved.

there exists neither security nor auspiciousness, except through the propitiation of Hara.
Those from whose lips no words of devotion toward the feet of Śambhu have been uttered have been cast out;
their foreheads are bruised and their skulls shattered by hundreds of blows.

The renunciation ordained by Śambhu according to the prescribed rite has not been performed;
likewise, one has not reached the further shore of the great ocean of Śaiva knowledge in accordance with the rules.
The wielder of the trident has not been worshipped with flowers such as karṇikāras and tilakas;
this time has been spent by those intent on offering funeral cakes for others, like crows sent away [to feed].
The state of the Lord was not meditated upon according to the rules for the sake of severing the cycle of existence;
nor was the omnipresent Śambhu praised daily with the sacred scriptures on this earth.
Nor was worship ever performed for Śaṅkara with intense fragrances, incense, or flowers;
surely we were created here by the Creator without cause, merely to fill up the world.
Those by whom [the mantra] has been recited even for a moment at the lotus-feet of Śambhu— whether through association or out of curiosity—
pass beyond the three worlds of Brahmā, Indra, Viṣṇu, and the Lord of Wealth (Kubera).
He who, with a peaceful disposition, constantly bows down to Him who has withdrawn all creation,
is severed from the bonds of affliction and, free from passion, enters the radiant abode of Rudra.

Lakṣmī, with her lotus-hand raised toward her elder brother, circumambulates him who is steadfast.

the blue-throated Lord (Śiva), who has not yet been honored by other births with garlands of white *mālatī* flowers mixed with white water-lilies (*kuvalaya*), has now been worshipped by the three preceptors of the gods with such white garlands.
Deprived of both knowledge and wealth, their minds are restless, and their throats are parched with hunger and thirst;
corrupted by faults in this world, they are constantly subjected to humiliation and lack of prosperity.

Having taken clay and yellow pigment (*rocanā*), one should offer incense with mantras to the child;
then, together with its nails, the white and dark [teeth] should be worshipped with lotus flowers.
To the Lord of the Moon (Candrabhūpa),

one should offer as a sacrificial oblation (*naivedya*) meat from a Rohita fish, or goat, or likewise from a porcupine; and one should cause to be given various preparations of wheat and foods cooked in ghee.
With that [remnant], one should feed the daughters and also the twice-born, and ask them for forgiveness.
According to one's ability, a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) should be given, as well as that meal for oneself.
A person who eats before others have finished their meals obtains the merit of giving away a thousand cows;
such a person becomes healthy, happy, and blessed in this world.
One should proclaim the name of Durgā; he is honored in her world.
O Bhārgava, one should bathe with earth from the roots of *darbha* grass during the month of Kārttika.
Having bathed the goddess Kīrti with scented water and honored her with fragrant grasses (uśīra), one should anoint her;
incense made of the five essences should be offered, as well as lamps with sesame oil.
One should illuminate the offering of milk-rice with ghee; maidens and Brahmins should be fed,
and a blessing for well-being should be invoked, saying, "May Śivā be pleased," along with the giving of sacrificial fees.
By this method, O child, one obtains the fruit of the gift of knowledge;
becoming a knower of the truth of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, at the end of that, one attains the state of Śiva.
O descendant of Bhṛgu, on the eighth day of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, having installed the Goddess on the back of the mountain, one should then bathe in the waters of the sacred ford.
One should smear the child with soft earth from the eight mountains; one should worship with kuṣṭha, jātī, and gajāhvaya;
one should offer black agallochum as incense and present lamps of clarified butter.
One should worship with *pūṃja* and *kuṅkuma*; one should offer curd and cooked rice as the food offering (*naivedya*), and with that very same offering, one should feed young girls.
One should give a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) according to one's ability, and that constitutes the breaking of the fast for oneself.
May this speech of mine be pleasing; one shall obtain the fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice.
Right here one becomes wealthy and an enjoyer of pleasures, and at the end of the body, one reaches the station of Brahman.
On the eighth days of the month of Pauṣa, having bathed with the tips of *dūrvā* grass, wearing white garments,
having conquered anger and transcended dualities, one should bathe the Goddess with camphor water.
The wise one should bathe and anoint Śakra with māśīvālaka and sandalwood; he should burn incense and perform worship with blue *kurūṇṭaka* flowers.
One should offer an oblation of rice mixed with sesame seeds and jaggery, and by that means, one should feed young girls;
that act purifies oneself, and according to one's ability, one should honor them and cause them to recite prayers.
May the goddess Nārāyaṇī, who is ever-pleased, be gracious to me;
by performing this rite for the lord of planets, one shall obtain the abundant fruit of great charity.

O Śakra, one obtains the fruit of all sacrifices; there is no doubt in this matter.

One should offer fruit and sacrificial food (naivedya), avoid sorrowful meals, and provide for maidens;
one should perform these acts for oneself and cause the recitation of the benediction (svasti) and the giving of priestly fees (dakṣiṇā).
May Vijayā be the constant bestower of happiness upon me and fulfill my desires;

One who is joined with latent impressions (vāsanā) perceives the world as consisting of the Goddess;

Milk, sugar, and food offerings, as well as feeding of maidens and Brahmins, and likewise one's own breaking of the fast; one should announce the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) according to one's ability.

O Bhārgava, by this one obtains the merit of bathing in all sacred fords (*tīrtha*);
at the end, one goes to the world of the Sun and becomes equal to that planet.
On the eighth day of the month of Jyeṣṭha, the wise man, having renounced all attachments, should bathe with sesame seeds and worship the Goddess with water infused with nutmeg.
One should bathe and anoint him with that fragrant sandalwood;
thereafter, Vijayendu, the best of planets, should worship him with flowers.
The food offering for the Goddess consists of groats, and sugar is likewise offered to the maidens;
a sacrificial fee should be given according to one's ability, and one should have the Carcikā hymn recited.
One obtains the fruit of a Śukra-sacrifice equal to that of the Sautrāmaṇi;
on the eighth day of the month of Āṣāḍha, one should bathe [the deity] with water from a night-stream.
Then, having bathed the goddess with water and liquid,
one should smear her with camphor, sandalwood, and the waters of *rocanā*.
One should offer incense made of sandalwood, camphor, bālaka, asita, and śalyaka,
along with whatever auspicious things there may be, filled with sugar, out of devotion.
One should cause the Brahmins to give away the girl, as well as food for oneself;
a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) should be given according to one's ability, and one should recite the mantra "mahiṣaghnī."
A garland of lamps made with ghee alone grants all desires;
one obtains the fruit of all sacrifices, the gift of land, and all sacred pilgrimage sites.
O Śukra, this excellent vow— the great Durgā-vrata— was performed by me, by Brahmā, and by Viṣṇu, desiring the welfare of the world.
In former times, he brought about the destruction of the planetary spirits with this [mantra],
as did the gods, asuras, yakṣas, nāgas, kinnaras, and humans.
O tiger among planets, just as he performed this with the Apsarases and women for the increase of his good fortune, you too should perform it according to the prescribed rite.
Even by merely hearing it, one obtains all desired pleasures;
a man gains his cherished goals, and even a barren woman gives birth to a son.

Thus ends the thirty-third chapter, titled "The Vow of Durgā," in the *Śrī Devīpurāṇa*, within the section on the Incarnations of the Goddess. Chapter Thirty-Four.
Īśvara said:

In that [temple], having offered bells, banners, parasols, canopies, and mirrors, as well as drums,
flutes, and the like, and constant musical performances; ||034:002||
O Goddess, listen now to the fruit of merit for him who thus proceeds toward one who knows the meaning of the scriptures and is a virtuous worshipper in the temple.
O dear one, having rescued ten ancestors, ten descendants, and twenty-one including himself,

Go where you, O lady, are honored as supreme and most highly revered;
there, having enjoyed delightful pleasures for the duration of an intermediate eon, [you shall attain liberation].
Furthermore, whoever shall come here from Kālādi shall become the sole sovereign of the earth,
accompanied by servants and mounts, together with his harem and retinue.
May he who is devoted to Carccikā not be hindered by the power of his past karma;

One who constantly honors the daughters of the twice-born, and who has mastered the meaning of the scriptures concerning the Goddess,
attains supreme goodness and shall, at the end, go to Śiva.

he shall then go to the world of Śiva, which bestows the fruits of all desires. ||034:009||

He shall obtain his desired wishes and go to the world of the Goddess;
listen as I relate here a story of what occurred in the past.

That greedy fisherman, a slayer of fish who lived without moral restraint, went to Nepāla-patana, O Śukra, to practice his trade of catching fish. (91) [In the *Piṇḍī*, it was: "There was a fisherman (*laba*); he was without conduct (*nirācāra*); he was a butcher (*vambhana*). (ka;

[The tree in front of the Goddess’s house; *ka* and *ga* have *prastutena*]—O child, one should perceive him there at that tree in front of the Goddess’s house; having gone to his own home, he returns there again after a period of time.
Then Karpara, having come from Ka, laughing and being made deformed and maimed,
departed after giving [the gift]; he died again among the Kolas and became a lord of the Gaṇas.
Citra, the lord of the Vidyādharas, who had reached the further shore of all branches of knowledge,
attained great prosperity even through a very small undertaking.
Thus, that goddess, endowed with devotion,
constantly emitted semen from her banner— which was adorned with small bells— out of her brother’s desire for union,
O best of wonderful beings.

possessing unimpeded power, you are the Lord of all the directions.
Likewise, O best of Brahmins, you too should be devoted to the Goddess.

The maiden, having fed the Brahmins with curd, milk-rice, and sugar,

The maiden is declared to be divine; indeed, the wielder of the trident (Śūlinī) is in the form of a maiden. As long as her womb remains intact, she is the Goddess, the slayer of the enemies of the gods.
The twice-born, Brahmā, Śiva, and Viṣṇu are the observers of their own vows;
when they are worshipped, O Śukra, all the gods are thereby worshipped.
Then, food should be given to the poor, the blind, and the wretched;
by dedicating it to the Goddess who is omnipresent, it shall become inexhaustible.
One should present an offering (*bali*) consisting of various foods, unbroken rice grains, curd, *dūrvā* grass, and sugar,
to all the spirits (*sarvabhūta*) in the ten directions.
Having likewise recited the *Jñānākavajraghoṇā* mantra, consisting of either twenty-eight syllables,
and having mounted a lion upon a pillar, one should utter all auspicious sounds.
Having placed the eight-syllable mantra of the Mistress, the great mantra of the sound of the Vedas, and the words *Kālikā* and *Carccikā*,

Having thus placed that great banner of the goddess, clothed and adorned with all ornaments, one should likewise place those of the remaining [deities].
The gift of a banner for Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Indra, Rudra, Soma, Sūrya, and the gods of heaven is considered a great gift, the best among all gifts.
O child, as long as the semen is not offered upon the pinnacle of the temple, so long shall that temple not bear the mark of the gods.
In whatever place this empty banner is always present, the great-souled bhūtas, nāgas, gandharvas,
and rākṣasas flee away and cause various kinds of afflictions.
Therefore, O King, for the sake of peace, white banners were always hoisted upon houses, gates, cities, towns, and mountains.
Indeed, there is no gift anywhere superior to the gift of a banner;
and for the Goddess, the gift of a lamp is both desired and nourishing.
Whoever offers a banner according to this rite, O Śukra,
that man shall attain all his desires and proceed to the state of Śiva.
Even by the mere sight or conversation with him, men devoted to sin are liberated from all their sins and go to heaven; of this there is no doubt.
And by this king, according to this ritual, the queen was marked with the signs of the conch,
the discus, the bull, the eye, the swan, the peacock, and the elephant.
One who possesses right conduct and maintains devotion shall raise a banner-pole with hair at its tip;
for such a person, O Śukra, there are neither diseases nor enemies in battle.
And there shall be no pain from wounds inflicted by weapons due to the raising of the victory banner.
Thus ends the thirty-fifth chapter, titled "The Ritual for the Gift of the Banner," in the glorious Devīpurāṇa.

victory to you, who pervade all paths, who are beginningless, indefinable, pure, and established in the Self; O you whose form consists of the meaning of the many principles (tattvas) arising from the support through the vital air— salutations to you!

Citi [is one with] Brahmā, Śiva, Sadbhāva, Sūrya, and Manu; likewise with Dakṣa, Prajāpati, Vyāsa, Devala, Asita, and Gautama.

"O gods, this entire world, both moving and unmoving, is pervaded by the Goddess.

and those beginning with Kiṣkindhikā, who is renowned as Bhairavī.

minerals, or gems, shall become a partaker of happiness.
She should be depicted in the lotus posture (padmāsana), or seated upon a lion or a staff-throne;

Thus ends the thirty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Sacred Sites," in the *Śrī Devīpurāṇa*, within the section on the Incarnation of the Goddess.

[Endowed with] Ka,

the Great Goddess was gratified by Paraśurāma at Mahodaya.

She dwells upon the seat above the head; her seat was fashioned by Rāma with the heads of universal monarchs (cakravartins). Furthermore, the goddess Khaṇḍamuṇḍā was worshipped by him as another form of her.
Having attained a divine state together with those who move among the constellations,
the goddess named Aghorā was likewise worshipped on Mount Malaya.

[By tradition] who were these ancient goddesses worshipped by the son of Jamadagni for the sake of destroying the great dharma of the Brahmins, he of immeasurable splendor?

there was a Daitya named Bala, possessed of great strength and prowess.

the gods, including Brahmā and others, were shaken from their positions in heaven.

You alone are the knower of the scriptures, our benefactor, and the eternal protector of Śakra;
become quickly a boat for us who are submerged in the ocean of doubt.
Thus questioned by the gods regarding the offering of the sacrifice, that Guru spoke these words.
Bṛhaspati said:

Furthermore, learn from me those who have passed away and those who exist now.
The Ādityas, Maruts, and Rudras are known as the sons of Kaśyapa.

having understood this entirely and without exception, one should constantly undertake dharma and the rest during the moments, instants, hours, fortnights, months, sequences, solstices, years, and so forth. 047.004.
O Pitṛs of all the gods, beginning with the planets, listen!
Those who are born from the seasons are to be known as the Pitṛs of the seasons (Ārtavās).
The Prapitāmahas are the fifty Ṛtus, the sons of Brahmā; they are of three kinds: the Saumyas, the Barhiṣadas, and the Agniṣvāttas.
O Mothers,
the Sun, the Moon, Mars, and likewise Mercury;
Jupiter, Venus, and likewise Saturn.
Rāhu and Dhūmaketu—these are remembered as the nine planets;
they are the eternal discerners of existence and non-existence for me within the three worlds.
The sun and the moon— these two orbs are planets that bestow solitude;
Rāhu is their shadow-planet, and the remaining ones are known as star-planets.
Soma is the lord of the constellations, and Divākara is the king of the planets;
Agni and Āditya are said to cook [the world], while Candramas is known as water.
Āditya is recited as Śambhu; one should know Umā to be Niśākara;
and Pitāmaha is to be understood as the third planet, Aṅgāraka.
The son of Kāśyapa is Sūrya, and Soma is remembered as the son of Dharma;
both are the preceptors of the gods and asuras, radiant and great planets.
Both these sons of Prajāpati, Śukra and Bṛhaspati, as well as the illustrious Budha, son of Soma, and Śanaiścara, the son of Sūrya.
Rāhu is known as the son of Siṃhikā, and Ketu is the son of Brahmā;
indeed, the Sun moves below all the planets.
The moon is situated above the sun;
above the moon is the circle of the lunar mansions (nakṣatras); above the lunar mansions is Mercury (Budha), and above Mercury is Venus (Bhārgava).
Above that is Aṅgāraka, and above him is Vṛhaspati;
above him is Śanaiścara, and above him is the circle of the Ṛṣis.
Above the sages is Dhruva, and above Māyā is the triple heaven (tridiva) located at Dhruva;
there is the abode of the Ādityas, and Rāhu sometimes follows the path of the Moon.
The comet (ketu) always moves forth, situated within the solar disc;
the width of the sun, however, is nine thousand yojanas.
Its circumference is three times its width;
the orb of the moon is recorded as being twice the width of the sun.
His mandala is twice as large as that of the sun;
the portion of Bhārgava is ordained to be one-sixteenth of the moon's.
Bṛhaspati should be known as having one-quarter less than Bhārgava;
Vakra and Saura are declared to have one-quarter less than Bṛhaspati.
Within the expanse of the Vajra-maṇḍala, their height is less than a quarter;
the constellations equal to that of Budha are all those which are short.
They are half a yojana in measure; nothing smaller than those exists.
Rāhu eclipses the sun, while at other times he eclipses the moon with his sharp-edged form.
Therefore, a planet is known to have a fixed measure, whereas a comet is remembered as being of indefinite size.
Bhūr is the world of earth (bhūr-loka), Bhuvaḥ is the heavenly world (svar-loka); these are called the three worlds.
Mahar, Jana, Tapa, and Satya—these are proclaimed as the seven worlds.
The earthly world is Bhūrloka; the intermediate space is known as Bhuvarloka; and the world in heaven is Svarloka.
The remaining worlds above these follow in their respective order.
For fire is indeed the lord of the element of shadow; therefore, he is the Lord of Beings (Bhūtapati).
Wind is the lord of the element of space; therefore, wind is the Lord of Space (Nabhaspati).
The Sun is the presiding lord of Bhāvya; therefore, the Sun is the Lord of Day.
Furthermore, the Gandharvas, Apsarases, Guhyakas, along with the Rākṣasas, [are his subjects].
Listen to all the inhabitants of the earthly realm, those who move in the intermediate space,
the Maruts with their seven groups, the Rudras, and likewise the two Aśvins.
All the Ādityas, the Vasus, and likewise the herds of cows [are gathered];
in the fourth world, Maharloka, dwell those who abide for an eon (kalpa).
The great fifth [tattva] is served by all the lords of creatures (Prajāpatis),
such as Manu, Sanatkumāra, and others, who are the sons of Vairāja.
In the first heaven dwell the Vasus, and likewise the cows and women; in the fourth world, known as Mahendra, reside those who live for a kalpa.
The fifth heaven is served by all the Lords of Creatures (Prajāpatis); [the sixth is] the abode of heat.
Indeed, in the sixth heaven are established these gods who awaken the deities.
Truth, indeed, is the seventh world for those who dwell in the state of non-returning.
The Brahma-world is indeed declared to have the characteristic of being unimpeded;
the sun is situated one hundred thousand yojanas above the surface of the earth.
Those ten [regions] extend up to the Dhruva, each being double the distance of the preceding;
the Dhruva is recorded as being one hundred million yojanas above the earth.
Twenty-three hundred thousand leagues above the triple world is said to be Megha;
it is situated at two hundred thousand and one thousand [additional] yojanas.
[The constellations, ka ga; the triple world, ka ga is said:
Now, each successive world-sphere is ordained above Dhruva;
[there dwell] gods, dānavas, gandharvas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, and pannagas.
The Kratūchardvas and the Vidyādharas— these eight are the divine origins (devayoni).
They reside in the center of the Brahmāṇḍa, and beyond them, it is enveloped in darkness.
From that, fire, wind, and space arise; from that, the source of the elements (bhūtādi) is said to emerge.
From that, the Great One (mahat) and the Primal Matter (pradhāna); from that, Nature (prakṛti) and the Spirit (puruṣa).
The Supreme Lord is to be known as Puruṣa, by whose power the universe is pervaded;
Śiva and Umā are considered superior even to the highest among the gods.
Thus ends the forty-seventh chapter, titled "The Motion of the Planets," in the *Śrī Devīpurāṇa*, within the section on the Elevation of the Three Worlds.
Chapter Forty-Eight.
Brahmā said:
Rākā and Anumatī are the two kinds of full moon;
likewise, Sinīvālī and Kuhū are the two kinds of new moon.
The ray of the sun named Amā is established in the world of the moon;
because the Moon dwells therein, it is therefore known as Amāvāsī.
When the moon, divided into its digits as previously described, is full on the night of the full moon, it should be known as Pūrṇimā; and when the sun has set, it is called Anumatī.
Because the deities, together with the ancestors, favor her,
she is therefore named Tanumatī, and that full moon day is likewise so remembered.
[The first case:
When the sun has set and the full moon rises simultaneously, that northern night is *rākā*, preceded by *anumati*. (048.005)
When the moon is full at its setting, the gods together with the ancestors approve of that night; because of the moon's delight, the poets have called it *Rākā*. (048:006)
Sinīvālī is said to be the measure when the moon has waned and only a remnant remains;
she enters the sun on the new moon day (amāvāsyā), and is therefore known as Sinīvālī.
The time that elapses when the cuckoo utters its cry is designated by that specific name; indeed, this new moon day is known as Kuhu.
Kuḥ, he, ka, pa, l, kt, ā, stu, ka, anu, ma, tyā, sa, rā, kā, yā, si, ni, vā, lyā, and kuḥ—excluding huṃ:
for these, the time is two and nine (twelve); thus Ku-mātrā is known as Kuḥ.
The Sun increases the sixteen digits of the Moon during the bright fortnight;
during the dark fortnight, O Kṛṣṇa, the deities drink the nectar in succession by means of falsehood.
Vahni drinks the first digit, Tapana the second,
the Viśvedevas the third, and Prajāpati the fourth.
Varuṇa drinks the fifth, and Vāsava drinks the sixth;
the divine Ṛṣis drink the seventh, and the eight Vasus likewise drink the eighth.
Indra drinks even the ninth digit of the dark fortnight;
the Maruts drink the tenth, and the Rudras the eleventh digit.
Candra drinks the first digit (kalā) on the twelfth day, Viṣṇu and Dhanada drink the second digit on the thirteenth day,
and Paśupati constantly drinks the fourth digit on the fourteenth day.
Then the ancestors drink the fifteenth digit;
when that digit remains as a residue and has been consumed, it enters the solar orb.
When it enters the Amā ray, it is therefore known as Amāvāsī.
In the forenoon it enters the mountain peak; at midday, however, it enters the lord of the forest.
In the forenoon he enters into fire; at midday, however, he enters into the forest;
in the afternoon he enters into the waters, for he is born from water, his own source.
Having entered the waters with a single remaining digit, Soma produces grasses,
shrubs, creepers, trees, and medicinal herbs.
In the afternoon, when the medicinal herbs have ceased their activity and the cows graze and drink water,
the essence following within those limbs of the herbs passes into the state of milk through the cows.
