relying on the Bhaujaṅgī lunar day until the conjunction of the moon and the sun.
Having reached the constellation Āsādha (Śravaṇā), one should offer the funeral rice-ball (piṇḍa), but one should exclude the eldest son;
this applies to those who have perished in battles, or by water, fire, or by leaping from a precipice.
On the fourteenth day, there should be worship with fire, deer-skin, and vessels; on the new moon day, it is performed according to one's desire.
When the sun is situated in Virgo, one should perform worship on the eighth day of the bright fortnight during the day.
Having fasted, one should commence the worship of the Goddess at midnight with extensive and magnificent offerings, during the constellation of Rohiṇī or Śatabhiṣaj.
In the constellation of Rakṣarkṣa (Mūla), the slaughter of sacrificial animals and likewise the killing of venomous serpents should be performed; furthermore,
an offering of oblations to the Rakṣasas must be made for the pacification of all.
The chariot procession that was proclaimed of old should be performed;
during that great festival of supreme merit, one should worship the Goddess.
When the moon is situated in Libra, worship should be performed by the high-souled one through the offering of lamps;
lamp-trees should be fashioned, as well as other lamp-circles.
A pilgrimage to the Ganges should be undertaken for great fruit on the fourteenth day and on the new moon days;
likewise, O child, it should be performed on the first day of the lunar fortnight, for then it yields great fruit.
At the very end of Śinīvālī,
the wise person should perform the offering, worship, fire-sacrifice, and festival; the wise one should also perform the dismissal of the deities during the Pauṣṇa constellations.
A great festival of the *gandharva*-lamp-offering (*gaurājana*) should be performed for men, elephants, horses, and other beings;
on the full moon day of Kārttika, one should always cause worship and a sacrifice dear to the Goddess to be performed.
Worship of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and the other deities there yields great fruit;
one should perform the rite of releasing cows or set free a dark-colored bull.
O Brahmin, one shall obtain the fruit of all sacrifices without hesitation;
therein, the worship of the weapons must be performed for the sake of attaining all perfections.
On the path, one should perform the auspicious worship of Ahirbudhnya;
on Mondays and Sundays, one should perform the worship that bestows the fruits of all desires.
Under the Puṣya asterism, the Puṣyābhiṣeka should be performed, and one should worship Jayā;
on the fourth day of the bright fortnight of Māgha, the Mahāpūjā is ordained.
On the full moon day of Māgha, worship should be performed; one should indeed worship the goddess Maṅgalā.
In Phālguna, one should worship the goddess who is known as Caṇḍikā.
In that regard, worship of the Mothers is especially prescribed;
thus the Goddess is omnipresent, abiding within the bodies of all the gods.
When worshipped according to the prescribed rite, O child, she grants all desires.
Thus ends the fifty-ninth chapter, titled "Praise of Worship," in the *Trailokyābhyudaya-pāda* of the glorious *Devīpurāṇa*.
[In this *Abhyudaya-pāda*, the sequential worship is concluded.
Chapter Sixty.
Manu said:
Merit equal to that of an Aśvamedha sacrifice is obtained by the ritual release of a bull on the day of Revatī in the month of Āśvina, or on the full moon day of Kārttika.
A marriage may be performed on the full moon day of Phālguna or even on the full moon of Caitra;
however, the auspicious rite for Śivā on the third lunar day of Caitra yields great fruit.
Śiva said: "The sacrifice of the Aśvattha and Udumbara trees should be performed according to the rite of marriage;
it should take place at a sacred ford (tīrtha) with an arched gateway, or even in a cow-pen."
There are four auspicious heifers, or two, or even one;
the calf is complete in all its limbs, and that cow is red.
O Sage, having adorned Vatsikā according to her beauty, you should cause her to be given away;
O child, let there always be a single marriage with Nīla. (060:005)
It bestows the fruit of the horse sacrifice (Aśvamedha) even through a bull;
for if even one son goes to Gayā, many sons shall be born.
Or one should perform the horse sacrifice, or release a dark-colored bull;
that bull which is red in color with a face the color of a conch shell, [is suitable].
The bull Rohiṇeya has hooves the color of a conch shell; he is indeed known as the Blue Bull (Nīlavṛṣa), for his tail and head are marked blue.
Having first decorated him with marks, one should then adorn him completely with garlands.
Having marked it with *oṃ*,
one should draw a wheel on the left and a trident on the right using molten metal;
one may etch it with gold or even with iron.
By performing it in this manner with the burden of violence, one obtains the fruit proclaimed for the horse-sacrifice (vājimedha).
O child, whoever releases the calf for that purpose obtains it without a doubt.
Just as the unborn image of Śiva, when worshipped, grants all desires,
so too, by reciting [the mantras of] these three deities, one obtains infinite fruit.
Whatever merit is gained from worshipping Maṅgalā, as well as the fruit born of the gift of a cow,
one obtains all that, along with the merit of a thousand sacrifices, through the ritual release of a bull.
On the path, the eighth day dedicated to fragrance bestows the fruit of the Gandharvas; by means of the release of a bull, one obtains the merit of a thousand sacrifices.
The Kṣīrāṣṭamī is of great merit and bestows the fruit of the world of the Moon.
With curd one goes to the station of Viṣṇu; with an oblation, to the solar orb;
with honey, to all the deities; and with food prepared from śāli rice, to Śiva.
Sarvamaṅgalā bestows blessings through offerings of wild rice;
she shall grant all desires right here in this very world.
Worshipped in the east, the auspicious goddess grants all that is desired by the worlds;
she bestows even cherished things throughout the realm of the gods from every side.
O Great Sage, among acts of public utility— such as water-stations, groves, ponds, and temples—
even among those meritorious works, the gift of gold is most desired.
If an obstacle arises when the designated portions for the well and the grove have been prepared,
then it should be performed on the lunar days (tithis) such as Durgā and others, which grant all desires.
O Great Sage, regarding the gift of fire-offerings (*homa-dāna*) at the beginnings of the eons (*yugādi*):
it is on the third day of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha, the ninth day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika,
the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight of Nabhasya (Bhādrapada), and the fifteenth day of Māgha.
During an eclipse of the moon or the sun, one should offer that [food], as well as the eightfold body and the two solstices;
even water mixed with sesame seeds should be given to the ancestors by a man who is self-restrained.
"Faith has been practiced by him for a thousand years"— this is a secret that the ancestors declare.
And at these times, whatever gift, oblation, or relinquishment has been offered with effort by the Creator, its merit is augmented.
The sages declare that he is praised in the Vedas and sung by gods and perfected beings throughout infinite eons.
Alternatively, O Great Sage, this meritorious rite for the restoration of the worn-out [mantra] should be performed for deities and others by those desiring the fruit of great enjoyment.
The merit in one who restores a ruined [stūpa] shall be eight times that of the original merit.
Therefore, O Sage, one should perform the consecration of dilapidated [shrines] that are without a protector,
whether they belong to oneself or to others, with extensive rites according to one's means.
Whoever adorns the deities, whether by his own effort or through others,
shall remain happy for as long as the moon and sun exist in the sky.
Among those worlds, his intellect was detached from the gods;
for as many years as there are hairs on the body of an animal in the Gomedha sacrifices, he remained with a mind fixed upon them.
Free from passion, with a joyful soul, he dwells in heaven as one who has brought the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) to their end.
Whether they are without a protector or have a protector, the gods are always worthy of worship.
When the world was free from passion and likewise devoid of dust, where were they?
But especially those who existed before, O Sage, they should always be worshipped—
Pṛthu at the beginning of his striving, and Umā-Śaṅkara on Mount Maināka.
Yayāti worshipped Śaṅkara on Mount Gomanta along with Hari,
and in ancient times, Raghu worshipped Ardhanārīśa on Kailāsa.
Likewise, while the three forms were established in the kingdom by Dilīpa, who desired them,
even the sacrificial fee was obtained; having worshipped the Goddess here, the desired fruit was attained.
Other sages as well attained perfection through the performance of pūrtta deeds.
Thus ends the sixtieth chapter, titled "The Ritual for Worship," in the *Śrī Devīpurāṇa*, within the section on the Incarnations of the Goddess.
[In the first incarnation of the Goddess, the ritual for worship (ka ga).]
Chapter Sixty-One.
Brahmā said:
O child, at the beginning of this, you should perform my worship according to the prescribed rite,
with offerings of perfumes, incense, and worship, as well as with garlands made of *damana* flowers.
One should worship the God with this oblation; one shall obtain all desires, and that person attains the fruit of bathing in all sacred fords.
On the second day, one should worship Umā, Śiva, and Hutāśa;
first, offerings of fragrant substances, oblations, sacred mantras, and food should be presented.
O best of Brahmins, one obtains that fruit which was proclaimed by Umā;
on the third lunar day, one should worship the Goddess together with Śaṅkara.
[Regarding what was spoken concerning the meteor:
[One should worship her] adorned with saffron, agallochum, camphor, jewels, garments, and garlands; and with fragrant flowers, incense, and well-woven damana blossoms. ||061:005||
O child, if one swings on a swing decorated with flowers, Śiva and Umā are forever pleased.
One should perform a vigil at night, and in the morning, a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) should be given.
Gold ornaments, garments, vessels, betel leaves, and garlands should always be used by women who desire good fortune and the happiness of having sons.

Having prepared the retinue of garments, seats, and bowls, one who is filled with devotion should perform worship to Gaṇeśa with sweetmeats such as *laḍḍukas* on the fourth lunar day, for the destruction of obstacles and the fulfillment of all desires.
On the fifth day, one should worship the nāgas and the great serpents (mahoragas) beginning with Ananta;
milk and ghee should be offered as the food-offering (naivedya), which removes all poisons.
On the sixth day, an infinite number of offerings should be made; worship accompanied by all types of oblations must be performed for Skanda.
In this very life there will be happiness and good fortune, and at the end, one shall go to the city of Skanda.
Having performed worship of Bhāskara on the seventh lunar day with *damanaka* and other offerings, one who has great ascetic power and is free from enemies attains enjoyments and other blessings.
O child, by performing on the eighth day a worship dedicated to all purposes and involving perfumes for the Mothers, one obtains the desired accomplishment through *damanaka* flowers.
On the ninth day, one should worship the Goddess Mahāmahiṣamardinī with all kinds of food,
perfumes, and desires, using saffron, agallochum, camphor, incense, food, banners, and mirrors.
By means of *damanaka* flowers and *marūpa* leaves, one obtains the fruit known as victory;
on the tenth day of the month of Kārttika, worship should be performed for Dharmarāja with fragrant substances.
Free from enemies and devoid of fear, one attains the supreme state here at the end;
on the eleventh day of the month of Vṛṣa, worship should be performed with all offerings.
Possessing fragrance, wealth, and sons, O beloved one, he is honored in the world of Viṣṇu;
on the twelfth day, one should worship Viṣṇu with camphor, agallochum, and sandalwood.
O mighty-armed one, by eating sacrificial food (haviṣya), one shall attain the station of Viṣṇu;
on the thirteenth day, Kāmadeva should be worshipped according to the prescribed rites.
Endowed with delight and joy, and adorned with *aśoka* flowers and jewels,
he should be depicted upon a water-pot or a white cloth, together with leaves, fruits, and other such items.
By offering oblations of sugar-candy, one shall obtain incomparable good fortune.
On the fourteenth day, [one should worship] the Lord of Gods, whose crest is marked by the crescent moon.

Having bathed [the deity] with ablutions of milk and other substances, one should worship it according to the rules with incense, flowers, fragrances, and *damanaka* flowers accompanied by fire-offerings (*homa*).
O Śivā, one should perform great worship with garments, food, and jewels set in gold;
a canopy, banners, and a parasol should be offered, and a vigil must be observed.
One obtains great merit, exceeding that of a hundred horse-sacrifices;
likewise, it should be performed on the full moon day for the fulfillment of all desires.
One obtains the desired fruit for Indra, who is joined with Śacī;
thus it is for whoever performs worship for fifteen days.
One shall obtain the fruits of all sacrifices, austerities, and gifts;
one sports at will in heaven amidst the diverse enjoyments of the gods.
"Having come here from the exhaustion of his merit, he becomes a king upon this earth;
he will be free from enemies— of this there is no doubt," so said the Blessed Lord Śiva.
Thus ends the sixty-first chapter, titled "The Worship of Damanaka," in the *Śrī Devīpurāṇa*, the Great Manifestation (*Mahābhyudaya*).
[End of the Worship of Damanaka in the First *Mahābhyudaya*].
Chapter Sixty-Two.
Brahmā said:
In the month of Vaiśākha, worship should be performed with garlands made of *pāṭala* flowers;
likewise, in Jyeṣṭha, one obtains all desires through *padma* and *arjuna* flowers.
In the month of Āṣāḍha, one obtains the desired fruit by offering bilva and kahlāra flowers.
For us, worship with jasmine flowers shall not be fruitless; it shall yield great results.
In the month of Āśvina, she is adorned with Kadamba and Campaka flowers and bestows the fruit of all desires.
Worship with two garlands of lotuses bestows all prosperity;
worship with a hundred-petaled flower in the month of Kārttika fulfills all desires.
On the path that leads to all accomplishments, worship with blue lotuses is performed in the month of Puṣya; likewise,
worship with water-lilies in Māgha bestows all desires.
In Phālguna, the Mādhavī [flower] arising from the Maru region bestows auspiciousness;
likewise, O best of planets, he who should perform [this rite] with the Caitrī [flower] throughout the entire year [shall obtain the same].
Listen to the fruit of merit for one who offers perfumes, flowers, food, and clothing;
one obtains the fruit of the gift of gold, land, garments, food, and knowledge.
The fruits are, respectively: the Vājapeya, the Mahāmedha, the Rājasūya, more than a hundred [offerings], the Aśvamedha, the Paśumedha, and the Gomedha.

One obtains the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) for the oblation; at the conclusion of the vow, one should offer it according to the prescribed rite, along with a fulfillment consisting of fruits and flowers, as well as garments, silk cloths, garlands, and food.
Gold, land, cows, clarified butter, milk, curd, and cooked rice—these grant the fruit of all desires.
Thus, whoever should perform worship in accordance with their disposition, [attains success]. ||062:009||
O child, he who always dwells in the abode of Śiva shall become Śiva himself.
Thus ends the sixty-second chapter, titled "The Worship of Images," in the glorious Devīpurāṇa.
[In the first [part], the worship of images.]
Chapter Sixty-Three.
Manu said:
Brahmā questioned Śaṅkara, the Great God residing in Mandara:
"O Lord, in which various places are you to be seen by me?"
Īśvara said:
One should worship Mahādeva at Vārāṇasī, Maheśvara at Prayāga,
Devadeva at Naimiṣa, and Prapitāmaha at Gayā.
They know him as Sthāna in Kurukṣetra, Viśvarūpin at Prabhāsa,
Ayogandha at Puṣkara, and Viśva at Vimaleśvara.
At Aṭṭahāsa he performed the Mahānāda vow, and at Mahendra, the Mahāvrata.
One should worship Mahākāla in Ujjayinī and Mahotkaṭa in Mākoṭa.
Śaṅkukarṇa possesses great splendor, and Gaukarṇa possesses great strength.
At Rudrakoṭi there is the Mahāyogī; at Sthaleśvara there is the Mahāliṅga; at Harṣa there is Harṣita; and all is Madhyamakeśvara.
In Kedāra he is Īśāna; in Rudra, Mahālaya;
in Suvarṇākṣa, Sahasrākṣa; and in Vṛṣabha, Vṛṣadhvaja.
The wise know that in the *Bhairava* [pīṭha], which is called the Thousand-fold, it has the form of Bhairava; at the site of the weapon (*śastrapada*) it is Ugra,
and at Kanakhala it is likewise Ugra, while at the lake of Bhadrakarṇa it is Śiva.
In the Devadāru forest at Vastrāpada is Diṇḍi; in Madhyama-jaṅgala is Caṇḍa;
in Turuṇḍa is Urdhvaretas; and at the end of Sukalā is Kapardin.
[Daṇuṃ ga; Jaṅgama ga; Svaphalāṃ ga] And Kṛttivāsa, Ekāgra, Sūkṣma, and Abhratikeśvara.
One should worship Nīlakaṇṭha at Kālañjara and Śrīkaṇṭha at Maṇḍukeśvara.
The yogi [should worship] Dhyānasiddheśvara and Gāyatrī at Uttareśvara.
In Kāśmīra he is named Vijaya; in Marukeśvara, Jayanta;
in Hariścandra, Hari; and in Purīścandra, Śaṅkara.
One should know Jaṭī at Rāmeśvara, Saumya at Kukkuṭeśvara,
Bhasmagotra at Bhūteśvara, and Jaleśvara at Jalaliṅga.
One should worship Jalapriya in Gabhikṣuka, Vārāha on Mount Vindhya,
Tāmra during the western twilight, and Trilocana in Virajā.
They know Triśūlī at Tṛptīśvara, Tripurāntaka on Śrīśaila,
Kāla at Jala-liṅga, and Kapālī at Karavīraka.
In Dīptacakreśvara he is Veda; in Nepāla, the Lord Paśupati;
in Śrīkārā, Lakuṭi; and in Vedīkā, the Lord of Umā.
You are Vaktra-rekha at Gaṅgādevikā, Gaṅgā at the ocean, Amara at Amarakaṇṭaka, Oṃkāra at Saptagodāvara, Bhīma at Svayambhū, and Nakuleśvara.
One should worship Gaṇādhyakṣa at Karṇikāra, Bhūrbhuva on Gandhamādana,
Siddheśvara in the sky, and Hāṭakeśvara in Pātāla.
Sixty-eight names of the wise God of gods have been sung in the Purāṇa by the self-existent Brahmā himself.
The wise person who, having risen at dawn, whether bathed or otherwise pure, should recite this,
is liberated from all sins and goes to the world of Śiva.
Thus ends the sixty-third chapter, titled "The Proclamation of the Sixty-eight Names of Mahādeva," in the Śrī Devī Purāṇa.
[In this first Devī Purāṇa, the sixty-eight names of Mahādeva are contained.
Chapter Sixty-Four.
Brahmā said:
O Sage, having taken a bull and two heifers that are young, endowed with auspicious marks, with horns of gold and hooves of silver, and covered with cloth, one should worship them.
Having worshipped Śiva and Umā on that day, whoever offers [this] to a Brahmin devoted to Śiva under the asterism of Rohiṇī or Mṛgaśiras, [attains great merit].
There shall be no separation for him from his sons, wife, and husband;
indeed, O twice-born one, he shall go to the city of Śiva with honors, possessing the speed of the wind.
Having enjoyed enjoyments there for a long time,
he comes here and is born prosperous in wealth and grain, surrounded by sons and friends.
O Brahmin, by the power of this vow, one shall become free from enemies;
or, O Sage, he who honors a pair of cows accompanied by jewels [shall likewise attain this].
Whoever offers this pair of garments, may Śiva and Umā be pleased with that person of purified soul.
And being liberated from all evil and from sufferings, he sports forever.
In this world he shall be blessed, and at the end of the body, he shall attain the supreme state.
Thus ends the sixty-fourth chapter, titled "The Vow of the Cow-Jewel," in the glorious *Devīpurāṇa*.
[In some versions, this is titled "The Vow of the Cow-Jewel for Prosperity."]
Chapter Sixty-Five.
Brahmā said:
On the third day of the bright fortnight, one should draw [the deity] upon a pair of auspicious cloths using yellow pigment, black ink, and saffron; thereafter, one should worship Śiva and Umā.
O child, with garlands of gold and jewels, one should recite the pair of mantras;
that which was previously proclaimed is the Nadamana-mantra Śaṅkha.
Therefore, O best of the twice-born, one should perform recitation, worship, and fire-offerings;
this king of vows is always beneficial for ensuring that women are never separated [from their husbands].
One should cause a thousand new *ga* [coins], made of gold and enriched with jewel-like flowers, to be offered as a burnt oblation (*huta*).
This bestows great merit and great fortune, and grants all desires. ||065:004||
O twice-born one, by that [rite], there shall be no separation from one's sons or brothers;
nor shall there be disease or calamity, O sage Tanturaja, for as long as the lineage lasts.
For that duration, he joyfully sports for a long time within the vision of Umā.
A blade of grass the length of a handspan should be placed between the thumb and the forefinger. 065.006.
Having kindled [the fire] until it is fully ablaze, one should begin the meal;
having worshipped the Goddess, one who is purified by the sixteen [syllables] should proceed.
By worshipping with golden flowers, perfumes, and various jewels according to the prescribed rule for a full year, one shall obtain all desires in accordance with righteousness.
O child, the ninth day is considered a festival when it is ablaze; it is deemed a gift of gold and cows.
By that rite at the conclusion of the vow, one becomes unconquered in battle. (065.009)
Just as Lord Maheśvara becomes [the protector] of a host of enemies,
so too [is it achieved] by this very procedure using either guggulu resin or pills.
Having worshipped Guggulu and barley with mantras, one should offer them into the blazing fire according to the ritual rules for Śivā;
the sacrificial fee here is as previously mentioned, and the fruit is that declared for the horse sacrifice.
Manu said:
For a king or a prince afflicted by the evil influence of the planets,
or for a queen whose children have died, [one should act] toward the twice-born or the king.
When the result of one who has exerted great effort and made diligent application turns out to be ruinous, and where the loss of elephants, horses, cattle, and bulls occurs; ||065:013||
Wherever portents are observed on the earth or in the atmosphere,
there a wise man should perform the great yoga of the Puṣya-consecration.
The king is declared to be the root, and his subjects and so forth are the branches;
through the cultivation of injury toward them, whether auspicious or even inauspicious, [the result follows].
"O child, effort must always be exerted; the root is the source of the branches and so forth.
When the root is destroyed, the branches and the abundance of fruits perish."
Therefore, O Great Sage, one should strive for the protection of the root-meaning;
for that indeed serves as the cause for attaining dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa.
O Śaunaka, listen as I proclaim to you that peace which was formerly expounded by Bṛhaspati for the sake of Mahendra, as directed by Brahmā. 065:018.
A bath during the Puṣya asterism is likewise meritorious, destroying all sins;
it is divine and pacifies portents—understand that this is where the ritual should be performed.
[Great merit; where should it be established? Where?
On a patch of ground free from anthills, husks, hair, bones, thorns, and gravel; smooth, very moist, odorless, and devoid of pits. (065.020)
In a very beautiful place free from herons, pigeons, vultures, owls, and the like, where there are *carmakāśoka*, *vakula*, and clouds-like thickets of grass.

In a most pure grove of young trees, entwined with spreading creepers and possessed of unblemished leaves; in a place abounding in trees, exceedingly sweet and adorned with fruits and sprouts. ||065:022||
It was crowded with flocks of fledglings, graced by the cries of cocks,
and filled with jīvañjīvaka birds, hārītas, woodpeckers, and parrots.
O child, make it a *cakora* bird, or perhaps one graced by *cakravāka* ducks; O peacock, O *pārāvata* pigeon, O *koka* ruddy goose, resound with the song of the cuckoo! (065.024)

In a forest region, or in an auspicious field or grove, one should perform the sacrifice— a place crowded with bees intoxicated by drinking the honey-wine of flowers and filled with six-eared creatures.
One should offer oblations of liquor made from fragrant flowers at the Himālaya, or as far as the Sahya or the Vindhya mountains,
or else on the sandy banks of rivers or at delightful confluences.
In the sand and mud, there were scratches from the claws of water-birds;
it was filled with the songs of *kāraṇḍava* ducks and cranes, resembling a canopy of soaring swans.
O Thousand-eyed One, I begin [this hymn] to her whose eyes are like blue lotuses;
she whose face is a blooming lotus, born of a noble lineage, and who speaks with the voice of a swan.
With breasts like freshly blossomed buds, dwelling upon lotus leaves,
her hooves were covered in the dung produced by the churning of the mountain, amidst the tumultuous sound of foam.
O playful one,
where the sons of Ka are complete with the sound of *huṃ*, and which is graced by the excellent calf;
there on the shore of the ocean, one should perform the rite where the sons have arrived.
Those of pure nature dwell free from agitation in treasuries filled with jewels,
or on the outskirts of their own blue *nicula* groves, frequented by birds.
Where lions, boars, and elephants dwell together upon the mountain, and where birds and deer live in harmony; ||065:032||
One should always perform one's bath there where the auspicious abode of the Mothers is located,
where women are languid with the weight of their hips and thighs, adorned with girdles, tinkling ornaments, and anklets.
Or where, O Mātanga, there is a woman languid with passion in her gait, illustrious, with eyes like a deer's, and speaking with the voice of a cuckoo.
O Sage, one should perform it in whatever house one dwells with joy, or even elsewhere.
[She who bestows flowers from others],
on the ground where water flows from the east, on the path of circumambulation among people,
with jackals and mongooses at the head, and devoid of the finest *kevika* and *karkaṭī* plants.
Possessing the [proper] colors, scents, and tastes, dense, smooth, even, and auspicious;
it has been repeatedly examined for signs of germination from seeds and other such defects.
Having gone there at an auspicious moment, one should perform the consecration (adhivāsana) in the north.
One should present an offering of flowers along with the recitation of mantras, saying:
"May all the gods who desire worship come hither."
Having thus invoked the quarters, the twice-born, the mountains, and whoever else shares in a portion,
the domestic priest should then speak as follows.
Having received the worship tomorrow and bestowed peace upon the king, they shall depart;
then, after performing worship for them, he should remain there that night.
Sleeping in a mouse-hole, seeing a cow-calf, curd, or the body of a deity;
and seeing dūrvā grass, unbroken rice, jewels, fruit, or mountains— these bring victory.

In that enclosure, one should dwell; the sight of *dūrvā* grass and so forth, as well as the sight of an umbrella, chowries, a conch, a lotus, white garments, and the like, are proclaimed to be for the fulfillment of all desires. ||065:042||
Fruit-bearing, flowering, creeper-clad, and milky trees are considered to bestow auspiciousness;
climbing upon them is most excellent when performed on temples, bulls, and similar objects.
An eclipse of the moon or sun is auspicious, as is climbing a mountain;
being bound by fetters in a dream brings victory over one's enemies.
If an enemy should overturn a mountain, conceal his voice,
or encircle a palace, he who performs these with a focused mind shall achieve victory.
Weeping for the deceased, as well as arriving and departing, brings about auspiciousness.
In a dream, however, crossing over wells, mud, or pits is auspicious;
likewise, crossing rivers and crossing the ocean is praised.
Having conquered the enemy army, a man attains victory;
he receives ornaments such as bracelets and other finery, and gains the happiness of a kingdom with sons.
Friends, people, lutes, gains, women, and those who bestow wealth;
yet he who drinks blood, or if he should ever cross over [the river], [is freed].
If one eats [the food] beginning with the month, or if it is obtained as a gain, one attains the desired fruit;
laughter, dancing, enthusiasm, and teaching are the causes of strife.
A woman from the south, black-eyed, brings fear and death;
[dreaming of] a lotus, going upon a lizard, or entering a well.
In the north, there is a terrifying dream involving the arrival of those wearing red garlands and garments;
within one's own kingdom, there appear monkeys, crows, owls, boars, snakes, and naked mendicants.
Having observed the inauspicious [omens], recitation (japa) should be performed; those [remedies] derived from minerals do not yield fruit.
For ailments arising from wind, bile, and phlegm, [treatments such as] riding, fire, and crossing [water] are prescribed.
In summer, autumn, and spring, the humors (doṣas) do not become provoked nor yield their fruits;
this is observed when there is recitation of what has been heard, following upon what has been experienced and praised.
If they are not seen, or if they are seen at the first watch of the night, they yield middling results; but if seen at the end [of the night], they all bestow swift results.

Those [omens] which are seen during the release of the cows are likewise proclaimed; having seen auspicious dreams, one should perform a sacrifice, but one should not cause [inauspicious rites] to be performed.
One should undertake bathing, worship of the deity, fire-offerings (homa), recitation (japa), and rites for peace;
having done so, everything becomes auspicious, and thereafter one should draw the mandala.
Beginning from four cubits up to one hundred cubits, the mandala should be constructed there; beyond that, one should not have it made.
The Vimala, Vijaya, Bhadra, Vimāna, Śubhada, Śiva, Vardhamāna, Deva, Mandākṣa, and Kāmadāyaka palaces.
The *rūcaka*, the one called *svastika*, and the twenty-second—these are the mandalas;
the powders, beginning with white and ending with green, should be made very beautiful.
Ten [substances]—
rice, *ṣaṣṭika* rice, safflower, turmeric, and *haripatra*;
as well as gems and coral dyes— should be consecrated with ashes.
Having prepared a powder with white mustard seeds, incense, and other substances, the practitioner should cause it to fall;
then he should place the King of Weapons (Astrarāja) mantra, or even the *atipada* if available.
Having performed an auspicious rite of purification, one should smear the ground with cow dung and perfume it with the powder and incense of sandalwood, agallochum, and camphor.
The ground portion, well-measured and established, extending east, west, and north,
should be made level using svastikas, fish-marks, and so forth, by means of cords made from muñja grass or lotus leaves.
In the center, there is an eight-petaled lotus, which may be double or triple [the size];
the doors have equal lines, and it is radiant with a pericarp and filaments.
Likewise, one should perform the scattering of colored powders (rajaḥpāta) while holding a lotus, and similarly other auspicious signs such as svastikas and utpalas, with the right hand hanging down.
The middle, ring, and thumb fingers should be placed together as desired.
Having formed the downward-facing finger-gesture with ease, the wise one should cause it to fall.
But the line should be drawn continuous, uninterrupted, and free from clusters [of irregularities].
The wise practitioner should fashion [the tooth-stick] with a width equal to the joint of a thumb;
it should not be stuck together, uneven, too thick, broken, or covered in spots.
One should never draw a short [line] together with its extremity;
one should know that when they are joined there is strife, but when the sun and the enemy are crooked, there is a conflict.
If there are many lines, there will be disease; if they are excessively thick, there is constant suffering;
if they are mixed, one encounters danger from the side of enemies through the *bindu*s; of this there is no doubt. (065.070)
If it is thin, there will be loss of wealth; if it is severed, death is certain.
He shall suffer separation from his beloved, or from wealth and children.
If one should draw a mandala according to one's own whim without having understood [the rules], [there will be no success].
One incurs all the faults that were previously described;
therefore, one should draw an excellent mandala that is square and has four gates.
One should draw the lotus together with the gates according to the dimensions of the mandala;
O Brahmin, the lotus must never be made more than one cubit high.
A wise person should not write more than four [syllables] above; [for these represent]:
majesty, longevity, women, dharma, sovereignty, prosperity, beauty, and tranquility.
In the eastern gate of the mandala, there is the attainment of yoga and the acquisition of wealth;
as well as accomplishment, intelligence, fame, happiness, health, and being beloved by the people.
And the accomplishment of all desires and aims is in the northern door-maṇḍala;
[it grants] sons, longevity, strength, good fortune, and the crushing of enemies.
And the increase of sacrificial rites occurs in the mandala at the western gate;
in its center, moreover, is an eight-petaled lotus with a pericarp.

For a Brahmin, the stalk of the lotus should be four spans (vitasti) in length; for a Kṣatriya, it should be three spans; and for the others in their respective order, the stalk should follow that same sequence.
Taking recourse in the western direction, one should fashion the stalk.
The seven netherworlds (pātālas) along with their enclosures are proclaimed to be the limits of the worlds.
Such a lotus was fashioned by Śambhu, the god of gods,
together with banners and archways, and adorned with flags.
The pericarp shall be Mount Meru, and the hosts of planets are situated within the seeds;
the filaments are the rivers, and the mountains are situated upon the thorns.
The eight petals are said to be the directions; one lotus is firmly established there.
The seven netherworlds and the earthly realm are proclaimed to be its stalk.
The Bhūrloka is to be known as the petals, whose nature is the directions and whose sphere is the void.
The entire world is called the pericarp, and the three worlds are designated as the lotus.
At the time of worship, one should install the god Maheśvara upon the pericarp.
The Mothers, the Grahas, the Nāgas, the Yakṣas, the Rakṣas, the Divaukasas,
the Vasus, the Munis, the Lokapālas, the Rudras, and the lords of the worlds.
The lava-s, kāṣṭhā-s, kṣaṇa-s, yāma-s, and nights and days—both dark and bright;
the fortnights, months, seasons, years, yugas, and the intervals between yugas.
One should likewise draw the intermediate eons and the great eons upon the lotus.
In the first mandala, one should worship the god Śiva together with Vidyeśa.
One should worship him together with Gaṇanāyaka in the second enclosure.
One should place Bhāskara with the planets in the east, Pinākin in the northeast,
Keśava facing north in the south, and Pitāmaha in the west.
In the third [circle], in the forest of Maṇḍala, prepared at Bhedinī,
which is strewn with various mines of jewels, one should further paint the gods.
The family priest should cause the Nāgas, Yakṣas, Pitṛs, Suras, Gandharvas, Apsarases, Munis, and Siddhas to be placed in their respective positions.
The planets along with the lunar mansions, the Rudras, and the Mothers;
Skanda, Viṣṇu, and Viśākha, as well as the world-protectors and the celestial women.
Having prepared various pigments and ritual substances endowed with the qualities of fragrance,
the wise one should worship [the deity] with perfumes, garlands, and ointments.
They feasted on many various kinds of fruits, roots, and meats,
as well as on diverse and delightful drinks such as wine, milk, and fermented liquors.
A special worship was previously prescribed by me for the sacrifice to the planets; that same worship for the Mothers and the gods is now to be performed right here.
One should worship the Piśācas, Dānavas, and Rakṣas with meat and wine;
likewise, the Pitṛs with ointments, collyrium, sesame seeds, and meat.
The sages [honored] the serpents with the Sāman and Yajus hymns, with the fragrances of the Ṛgveda, with incense and garlands,
with the "three sweets," and likewise with all varieties of pigments.
One should satisfy the gods with incense, offerings of clarified butter, and precious gifts;
likewise, one should satisfy the gandharvas and apsarases with perfumes, garlands, and beautiful flowers.
But the remaining [deities] among those belonging to all castes, one should worship with perfumes and garlands,
as well as protective cords, banners, garments, and ornaments.
And for all of them, sacrificial threads (yajñopavīta) should also be given;
[these are placed] in the south, the west, or in the northwest of the mandala.

O child, having performed the fire-oblation (homa) as prescribed for the sacrifice to the planets and as declared in the rite for the Mothers, using these aforementioned materials endowed with the proper characteristics, ||065:099||
Parched grain, unbroken rice, clarified butter, honey, curd, milk, reptiles, white mustard seeds, fragrant flowers, incense, and sugar in abundance; ||065:100||
One who possesses passion should offer milk, snake-gem, gorocana, sesame seeds, darbha grass, fruits produced in their respective seasons, ghee, and milk-rice (pāyasa) filled with sauce.
On the western altar, this bathing rite should take place;
one should prepare very firm jars—their characteristics I shall now describe to you.
Thus ends the sixty-fifth chapter, titled "The Contemplation," in the *Śrī Devīpurāṇa*,
concerning the Mandala for the Flower Consecration in the first part.
Chapter Sixty-Six.
Brahmā said:
O Great Sage, I shall describe its origin, its characteristics,
and its measurement, as well as that which is proclaimed in the world as the obstructing *kalaśa*.
O reciter, when the nectar was being churned by all the gods together with the dānavas,
they made Mount Mandara the churning rod and Vāsuki the rope.
Therein, the nectar of great heroism and prowess has arisen from the [sacrificial] forms;
this jar is proclaimed for the purpose of containing it.
Since this jar was fashioned by the gods through Viśvakarman, having taken a portion from each of them, it is therefore called "kalaśa."
Brahmā is at the mouth of the pitcher, Maheśvara is at the neck,
Viṣṇu is situated at the base, and the hosts of Mothers reside in the middle.
All the remaining deities surround [it] on the four sides;
within its belly are the seven oceans, and the seven continents are situated therein.
All the constellations and planets, as well as the principal mountain ranges—
Himavat, Hemakūṭa, Viṣadha, and Meru itself.
The Rohita, Mālyavān, and Sūryakānti mountains;
the Gaṅgā, Sarasvatī, Sindhu, Subhagā, and Yamunā rivers.
The Erāvatī, the Śatahṛdā, as well as the river Vaitaraṇī,
the Godāvarī, the Narmadā, and the great river named Mahī.
Kurukṣetra, Prayāga, Ekahaṃsa, Pṛthūdaka, Amareśvara, Puṇḍarīka, and Gaṅgāsāgara as well; ||066:010||
The Aśvamedha sacrifice is within one hand;
whatever sacred fords (tīrthas) exist upon the earth reside within this water-pot.
Herein also dwell the pacification of the planets, nourishment, joy, and the Gāyatrī itself.
The Ṛgveda, the Yajurveda, and likewise the Sāmaveda,
together with the Atharvaveda— all are established within the pitcher.
Nor indeed are the auspicious jars originating from the form of Śambhu;
likewise, there are others such as the Marutas and the Samudas, produced from cows and those approaching cows.
Manohara is indeed proclaimed as the auspicious fifth;
both the sixth and seventh are Virajas and Tanudūṣa respectively.
The sixth is Talaiṣaṣṭa;
the eighth is Indriyopeta, and the ninth is known as Vijaya.
Nine indeed are the jars renowned; learn now their presiding deities.
The ninth, which is known by the name Vijaya,
is there Śiva himself, the auspicious remover of all sins, who dwells in person.
He is renowned in the world as the five-faced one, the accomplisher of all aims;
because he consists of the nature of the five Brahmās, he is remembered as the five-faced one.
One should know Sadyojāta to be in the western face, Vāmadeva in the northern,
Tatpuruṣa in the eastern, and Aghora in the southern.
Īśāna is the fifth, situated in the center above all;
these five faces, O child, destroy sins and annihilate the malevolent planets.
Sadyojāta shall be white, while Vāmadeva is yellow;
Tatpuruṣa is to be known as red, and Aghora is indeed black.
Īśāna is their western face, endowed with all colors; he is the granter of desires, capable of assuming any form at will, the support of knowledge, and identical with Śiva.
Kṣitīndra was the eldest, Kalaśa the second, Jalasambhava the third, Pavana the fourth, and Hutāśana the fifth.
The fifth is the sacrificer, while the sixth is born from space;
Soma is declared to be the seventh, and likewise the eighth is Āditya.
These eight forms of Indra, ending with Sūrya, were produced by the Goddess and formerly presided over by Śiva; they are the bodies of Śiva.
The Lord of the Earth (Kṣitīndra) is to be placed in the east; the one born of water (Jalasambhava) in the west;
Vāyu is to be placed in the northwest; and the one born of fire (Agnisambhava) in the southeast.
The lunar [mandala] should be joined on the north, and the solar [mandala] should be placed on the south.
Having thus performed the ritual placement (nyāsa), one should contemplate the primordial form of the vases.
Brahmā is indeed at the mouth of the jars, and Viṣṇu is at the neck.
Within his mouth are all the hosts of Mothers, along with the gods including Indra and the serpents;
in his belly are the oceans and the earth with its seven continents.
Śrī, Umā, the Gandharvas, and likewise the Ṛṣis,
as well as the five elements and the streams, are situated below them.
Filled with pure water, they are perfected and resplendent in every way,
whether by water from rivers, lakes, streams, or ponds.
The ponds and wells, filled with divine ocean water, bring happiness;
they are the most auspicious of all auspicious things and destroyers of all sins.
Such auspicious jars should always be taken for consecration,
whether at the time of a procession, a marriage, an installation ceremony, or a sacrificial rite.
These should be applied specifically as the accomplishers of all desires;
they are for that woman whose children have died, and for her who is proclaimed to be barren.
For those who have a dead fetus, those who are barren, those who are unfortunate, and those afflicted by disease—
the ritual bathing within a flower mandala should always be performed for them.
All kinds of jewels, medicinal herbs, fragrances, fruits,
and flowers should be employed during planetary afflictions, as well as for auspicious and propitious occasions.
Because they sustain the planets as well as various mothers and terrible misfortunes, they are therefore known as the "Sustainers" (Dhārakas).

Because the [proponents] maintain that they exist having withdrawn each individual digit (*kalā*) of the forms of earth and the other elements in due order, for that reason they are known as *kalaśas*.
Made of gold, silver, copper, or clay, and endowed with the proper characteristics,
they should be five finger-breadths in width and sixteen finger-breadths in height.
As for the measurement of the jars, the mouth should be eight finger-breadths wide;
he who is established as the eightfold form (Aṣṭamūrti) is Śiva seated upon a lotus.
The seven forms and the eight forms are his attendants; Śiva is situated upon its pericarp.
Those who are the attendants are the petals, those who are the serpents are the jars.
The jars are said to be the planets, and the directions are the world-protectors;
by these, this entire world, from the realm of Brahmā down to the earth, is pervaded.
By those great beings who are difficult to assail and who purify all sins.

Thus ends the sixty-sixth chapter in the glorious Devīpurāṇa, titled "The Description of the Origin of the Kalaśa, its Installation, and the Characteristics of the Deities. [End of the characteristics of the installation and the deities of the origin of the Kalaśa.]
Chapter Sixty-Seven.
Brahmā said:
One should place jewels, seeds, flowers, and fruits into the vase;
likewise, flower garlands and cloths at its end should be anointed with white sandalwood paste.
With diamond, pearl, lapis lazuli, great emerald, crystal, and all kinds of minerals; likewise with fruits such as the *bilva*, *nāraṅga*, and *udumbara*.
With citron, jambīra, mango, āmrātaka, and pomegranate;
with barley, śāli rice, nīvāra, wheat, and white mustard seeds.
[Sāmra, sāmrāta,
ga] kuṅkuma, aguru, karpūra, madara, rocanā, and candana;
where there is also māṃsī, elā, kuṣṭha, karpūra, and caṇḍāmba-rañjana.
Mātsya, aṣṭi, camphor, patra, paṇḍā, excellent water, jātipatra, kaṇa, gandha, pṛkkā, gaurī, and saparṇaka; along with vacā, rātri, mañjiṣṭhā, and turuṣka— this is the Maṅgalāṣṭaka.
Dūrvā, Mohanī, Mṛṅgāṅkā, Śatamūlī, Śatāvarī, Balā, Nāgabalā, Devī, Sahadevā, and Gajadhvarā. [The phrase "the fruit of sacrifice at Mount Udaśela" is not found in manuscript Kha. 067:006.
Bhagāṅga, gaṇḍharvahastaka, sahadevī, ajākṣī, māgadhikā,
pūrṇakośā, white pāṭhā, guñjā, surasikā, latā,
vyāpaka, gajadanta, śatapuṣpā, and punarnavā. ||067:007||
Having gathered the auspicious substances— brāhmī, the goddess śivā, rudrā, all types of fragrances, and gold— one should place them within the jars.
The two incenses, Kalyāṇa and Vijaya, are auspicious at moonrise;
likewise, the cloth known as Rocanā is adorned with all kinds of jewels.
With the intellect, [one should measure] two finger-breadths with the fingers, up to a limit of twenty-six finger-breadths;
it should not be an excellent square, nor should it have a lotus and moon as its inner core.
On the left are a lotus, a fish, the syllable *bhā*, a svastika, and Vināyaka;
[and] Śrī, Śrīvṛkṣa, Varāha, Hema, and these deities accompanied by auspiciousness.
[Not present in manuscript Kha] One should fashion a silk cloth adorned with all kinds of jewels, two cubits in length,
one cubit in width, and five finger-breadths in height, most beautiful to behold.
The one called *snāna* (bath) is one and a half cubits in length, provided with a cloth and a circular seat;
the one called *śayyā* (bed) is double that in length, measuring one bow (*dhanus*) and provided with a pedestal.

An elephant or a lion, displayed with majesty and adorned with gold and jewels—this is called the "Lion" [arrangement]; or else, it may be a pedestal for the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) measuring one and a half units in width.
Or a leaf made of gold, adorned with gems called *graha*,
and embellished with highly precious jewels known as *vajra*, *indranīla*, and *rudra*.
Alternatively, it should be made with four legs, or even symmetrical on all three sides;
one should have pillows fashioned from tiger skin, leopard skin, or bear skin.
Or else, one should prepare a well-characterized bed, four cubits in length, half that in width, covered with skins dyed by others or filled with soft cotton.
O Lord of Men, they desire [the length] to be more than one *vitasti* by means of the *kurū* measurement;
or else, O Gajasiṃha, it may be four, three, or two *padas*.
Or else, let the Creator raise up the trunk of a female elephant, variegated with ivory, adorned with gold and jewels,
and covered with an auspicious cloth.
The Kinnaras and others should be fashioned, endowed with all splendor,
possessed of auspicious bonds, along with water-jars and the planets.
The measurement should be made equal to a stone of Śiva; one should fashion the elephant of Śiva,
with a lotus, a svastika, a conch, a blue lotus, and accompanied by birds.
One should indeed perform the meditation on Śiva together with Śivopāyā;
where there is a well-constructed crown fashioned like a creeper, adorned with golden teeth and embellished with diamonds, rubies, emeralds, and lapis lazuli.
Having the shape of an elephant’s frontal globe or fashioned like a half-moon, it measures one thousand kinnarīs; and the seventh [measurement] is by hundreds.
Having drunk three hundred and twenty measures of the "human entrance" for all people,
one should prepare two quivers as a bed, filled with soft reed-grass.
The cushion should be variegated, made of gold, soft, and circular; one should fashion round, rhomboid-shaped earrings known as *śravaṇa* for the ears.
The vehicle should be fashioned in the form of a bed, with well-formed and beautiful legs;
it should be one span high, made of clay mixed with the earth from the foot of Śiva.
Having thus prepared the entire bedding, seat, and so forth,
enriched with the splendor of garments and ornaments, one should commence the consecration.
Then there was the unblemished hide of a deer belonging to the Vaiśya Dhūpa,
and after that, the third was that of a lion, followed by one of a tiger.
One should spread those four skins of the bull upon that sacrificial altar when an auspicious moment has arrived, and the moon is joined with the Puṣya constellation.
A throne (bhadrāsana) should be fashioned out of gold, silver, copper, or wood from a milk-exuding tree, measuring one and a half cubits in height.
The distance between the territories of neighboring kings should be one and a quarter *hasta*s;
with a well-joyful mind, the king should enter his bedchamber with a lamp during the winter season.

Surrounded by astrologers, ministers, chamberlains, bards, citizens, and friends, and accompanied by the sound of Vedic recitations from the twice-born, songs, and the resonant noise of skillful musical instruments; ||067:032||
Accompanied by the auspicious sounds of mṛdaṅgas, conchs, and trumpets, he struck the auspicious [drum];
he beheld the king clothed in unwashed silken garments and covered with a woolen blanket.
One should bathe [the deity] with jars rich in offerings and flowers, and filled with clarified butter.
Drink eight, sixteen, twenty, one hundred, or one hundred and eight [drops].
The enumeration of the jars is declared to increase progressively for those that follow.
The Goddess should then be bathed with auspicious mantras, or with auspicious recitations, or even with clarified butter (ājya) mixed with the ashes of Śambhu.
Clarified butter is declared to be splendor; clarified butter is the supreme remover of sin.
Clarified butter is the food of the gods; in clarified butter all worlds are established.
Whatever impurity has arisen— whether terrestrial, atmospheric, or celestial—
all that goes to destruction through contact with clarified butter (ājya).
Then, O King, having brought forth a woolen blanket and jars filled with water scented with flowers, one should bathe [the deity] while worshipping with this mantra: ||067:038||
May the gods consecrate you, as well as those who are the ancient Siddhas;
may Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, the Sādhyas, and the hosts of Maruts [consecrate you].
The Ādityas, the Vasus, the Rudras, and the two Aśvins, the best of physicians;
Aditi, the mother of the gods, as well as Svāhā, Siddhi, and Sarasvatī.
Kīrti, Lakṣmī, Dyuti, Śrī, Sinīvālī, Kuhū, as well as Diti, Surasā, Vinatā, and Kadrū.
May the wives of the gods who have been proclaimed, as well as the mothers of the gods and all the auspicious hosts of Apsarases, consecrate you.
The constellations, the auspicious moments (muhūrta), the fortnights, the days and nights, and their junctions;
The years, the days, the lords of the day, the kalās, the kāṣṭhās, the kṣaṇas, and the lavas.
May all the auspicious divisions of time consecrate you.
The hosts of gods dwelling in celestial palaces, human beings along with the oceans, the highly fortunate rivers, as well as the nāgas and kiṃpuruṣas; ||067:044||
The highly fortunate Vairājanas, those twice-born ones who move through the air,
the Seven Sages with their wives, and all those who occupy the fixed positions [of the stars].
Marīci, Atri, Pulaha, Pulastya, Kratu, Aṅgiras,
Bhṛgu, Sanatkumāra, Sanaka, and then Sanandana.
Sanātana, Takṣa, Jaigīṣavya, and Nandana;
Ekata, Dvita, Trita, Jāvāli, and Kaśyapa.
Kaṇva and Kātyāyana were likewise ill-behaved and ill-mannered.
Durvāsas, Garga,
Mārkaṇḍeya, Dīrghatapas, Śunaḥśepa, Vidūratha, Dvaipāyana, Saṃvartaka, Cyavana, Atri, and Parāśara.
Dvaipāyana, Yavakrīta, Devarāta with his younger brother—
these and other sages were devoted to the vows of the Vedas.
Let them, along with their disciples and wives, who are dense with ascetic merit, consecrate you;
let the mountains, the trees, and the holy sanctuaries be honored.
Prajāpati and Diti, cows— the mothers of the universe—
as well as divine vehicles and all the worlds, both moving and unmoving.
The fires are the ancestors, the stars are the living beings, and the sky, the directions, and the water [are the elements].
These and many others [attain this] through meritorious deeds and the auspiciousness of chanting [the Lord's names].
May they consecrate you with waters that dispel all calamities.
Thus, with these auspicious mantras, divine and likewise others, [he should worship].
By the Śaivas, the Nārāyaṇas, the Raudras, and those born from Brahmā and Śakra.
"Āpo hi ṣṭhā," "Hiraṇya," and likewise "Śaṃbhava."
The king, having sipped water for purification, should wear cotton garments that are auspicious among all auspicious things,
accompanied by the sounds of conchs, flutes, and musical instruments, and other auspicious rites.
Then one should worship the gods, the gurus, the brahmins, the banners, and the weapons;
one should carry the parasol, musical instruments, elephants, and horses, all of which have been consecrated with mantras.
Then, on the second day, the king went to the sacrificial altar, summoned the fire, and offered ornaments enriched with the *vijaya* powder provided by the god.
One should observe the faces, the positions, and the signs of the gods:
Svāhā to Rudra, Indra, Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and Śiva.
To the son of Prajāpati, to Kumāra, to the destroyer of obstacles, to Vināyaka;
