The lord of the ten families should know the proper time and the measure of wealth; for while one lives, the prosperity of the family reaches its peak among human beings.
No one should enter without having first inquired in truth about expenditures, marriage alliances, and the inheritance of property, nor should anyone allow an incoming visitor to enter.
One should understand both the cause and the time for liberation;
a guest from another region shall not stay for more than one night.
[The time of notification, etc.
Furthermore, when his business is flourishing at other times, there is simply no entry for him;
nor is merchandise brought from another region ever allowed to enter by the local residents. (072.092)
Indeed, they must provide a counter-commodity for what has been taken out;
this includes whatever goods are useful for the fortress, such as grain, bark, and so forth.
One should ensure that he has no means of subsistence, except in cases where he has been harmed by insects or similar causes;
for no one who is not supported should dwell there—not a bearer of the sectarian mark (liṅgin), nor a mendicant (bhikṣuka).
One should not allow those who bear weapons, nor the insane, nor the eloquent, nor actors and singers to enter;
nor should one admit strangers, but rather purify those who have already entered.
He should ensure that the gates are always kept unvacant by armed men,
and he should provide for the enjoyment of women who are not subject to their own desires.

[And for all those who come from afar, g. for all of them, ka] the sale of all commodities is permitted outside the slaughterhouses and on the main roads; likewise for one who has entered by a non-gate, or through a gate at an improper time. ||072:097||
The proclamation was made for the sake of prohibiting the use of fire by those with two feet, because of its constant occurrence.
And at the end of the rainy season, one should clear away the growth of grass from the pavilions;
one must not damage them with impurities, nor with pits, nor with household refuse.
One should not block the path of the outcastes with house-wood or grass;
a place for mutual viewing should be made from one station to the next.
One should signal by means of a designated object;
one should understand the path of the balance-beam.
At night, guards should patrol each individual section of the rampart wall.
These very same [feelings arise] when there is fear or apprehension, or even when the king has gone far away.
One should diligently establish continuous positions;
these should also be interspersed by soldiers and city-dwellers alike.
The scribes, characterized by their names, castes, lineages, and numbers,
[should record] each foot stationed at the rampart, moving everywhere.
One should station half of the army, clad in armor, in the center,
with those mounted on camels, horses, and mules who can travel swiftly over long distances.
Having thoroughly cleared the ground for ten yojanas around the fortress,
the high-minded one [should do so] wherever there is apprehension of danger.
Having learned the circumstances through spies, he should act appropriately;
[he should do so] with constant diligence regarding the treasuries and the granaries.
In the water-halls, those of noble birth, steadfast, and diligent should be employed;
likewise, servants who are fearful, greedy, terrified, addicted to vices, or deceitful [should be excluded].
In a fortress, officials addicted to gambling and intoxicants should not be appointed;
it must always be attended by a council of ministers and provided with physicians and astrologers.
And likewise, those who deal with snake-charmers and the like, as well as offerings consisting of poisons and such things.
The king should have Brahmins who are knowers of the Vedas present nearby.
One should avoid dogs and jackals at the great fortresses, such as the gate-towers and other such structures.
O Brahmin, when this is performed, one always obtains abundant prosperity—
prosperity that is enduring, accompanied by strength, free from obstacles, and attained with ease.
Vasiṣṭha said:
I wish to hear the true measurement of the gate-tower (gopura) in its essential nature; what kind of dimensions should be constructed, and on which days and lunar mansions (nakṣatras)?
Bṛhaspati said:
One should cause excellent gates to be constructed in great fortresses, starting from the east;
they should be thirty-two cubits in height and half that in width.
The second, the medium-sized [shrine], should have a height of sixteen cubits.
The third measure of Manu is half of that;
the fourth is the measure of Bhānu, and the fifth is the measure of Rudra.
The sixth should be made ten cubits; the seventh is honored as nine cubits;
O Brahmin, it should be eight cubits, and the eighth is considered to be from the door.
The wise man should construct doors with a width equal to half their height; the stone structures should have sturdy chambers and be equipped with various weapons.
[The palaces] were provided with upper galleries, walkways, groves, and the like;
they were furnished with royal audience halls and endowed with windows.
[He saw] vehicles for riding, such as those with rutting elephants, adorned with banners, with head-ornaments fashioned from elephants and serpents, and as beautiful as lotus petals.
One should have various doors constructed according to beauty and in due order; the middle [door] should be sixteen measures, or even half that measure.
The wise declare that for all fortresses, there must be a gate provided with doors,
bolts, and even door-sockets.
One should place eight iron spikes, well-arranged as "serpent-bindings" (nāgavandha) and equipped with mechanical devices, according to their respective positions.
One should cause the arm-chambers (bhujākula) to be constructed at the door-positions, as well as the doors and the intermediate spaces between the doors;
then the pavilion (maṇḍapa) and the walkway (vīthikā), where men bearing weapons [are stationed].
And gatekeepers stand there, always with weapons at the ready; one should have an image of Durgā, the slayer of the demon Mahiṣāsura, installed within the fortresses.
One should [worship] Gajavaktra (the elephant-faced one) stationed at the door, or Dhanada (the giver of wealth), or Padmaja (the lotus-born);
or else under the three Uttaras, Rohiṇī, or the asterisms of the gods.
One should cause the city gates and other structures to be built during an auspicious moment (sulagna) free from malefic planets,
or when [the lord of the house] is conjoined with or aspected by Venus, or during its period of exaltation.
One should perform the ritual offering (*bali*) during the laying of the foundation stones according to the rules prescribed for temples.
One should place a golden pitcher containing jewels beneath the branch [of the tree].
There, one should worship the seizing spirits (grahas) such as Pūtanā, Śakunī, Jambha, and others;
having worshipped the gods, sacrifices, grahas, and nāgas according to the prescribed rite.
One should honor the astrologers and the master builders with garments, oblations, garlands, and other offerings;
and having had the Brahmins recite benedictions, one should sacrifice an animal for the sake of peace.

One should cause a festival of various kinds to be held in the city for the sake of the Primordial Being of All Worlds, featuring curds, parched grain, garlands, a water-pot, and the four types of food, both solid and soft.
One should perform festivals and other celebrations with the sounding of conchs and drums;
likewise, the raising of a banner-pole should be carried out, along with a white umbrella and small flags.
Thus, the wise man, warding off the flow of desire for physical form at all gates,
should purify his eastern quarter when the moon arises in the constellations Svātī or Puṣya.
Because of that, O Sage, all other perfected ones were also utterly ruined;
those who were bewildered regarding the directions caused great harm to the king and the inhabitants of his realm.
One should construct a circular base made of udumbara wood,
with a diameter of one and a half cubits and a height of one cubit.
The wise man should fashion a branch that is either equal to the base or one-sixteenth of it; furthermore, a central door with three branches should also be made.
The pillars should be circular, numbering thirty-two, sixteen, eight, and eight; furthermore, they should be made square, according to their beauty and according to the city.
Having reflected upon the meaning as well as the treatise, one should establish the gate of the fortress; by this,
one quickly attains prosperity, free from fear and sorrow.
O Sage, when the proper gate is established, both the king and his subjects rejoice;
their common characteristic, as taught in the Sūtras, is praised everywhere.
Listen now to how it should be performed correctly in the cities and fortresses of Śaukra-ga,
so that he may enter like one mounted upon a supreme elephant, accompanied by a parasol.
Just as with the trees, so should the gates be constructed in the fortress to bestow dharma, artha, and kāma;
or else they may be made of iron— listen now to the detailed fruit thereof.
And above that, they are five [yojanas] in width, increasing successively from the eastward direction.
Excluding the eyes of men, those five which are broad and increase toward the right are considered auspicious.
The water [measure] is seven times seven; the subsequent [measure] is seven times five.
The gate-towers (gopuras) should always be constructed with an increase of five finger-breadths; however, if they are deficient in their length, they bring fear to the king.
The inhabitants dwelling within it are perpetually agitated and terrified by fear;
yet its gate-towers, with their well-proportioned foundations and limbs, always provide comfort.
I shall state their names, or as they have been proclaimed, [starting from] the shores of the waters.
Śrī, Kānti, Dyuti, Lakṣmī, Jayā, Bhadrā, Aparājitā,
Anantā, Śobhanā, and Durgā are proclaimed as being in the east.
Śānti, Vṛddhi, Bhavā, Devī, Kālī, Ghorā, Vimohinī,
and Vimalā— these are the gateways to the south that bestow auspiciousness.
Rocanā, Maṅgalā, Raudrī, Ugrā, Caṇḍā, Yaśovatī,
Prāpti, and Dīpti— these are the pathways of Vāruṇī that grant all desires.
Icchā, Prīti, Śubhā, Mātā, Yaśodā, Dhanadā, Umā,
and Śaraṇyā— these are considered the Gopurikās in Durgā by virtue of their gentle nature.
It should be well-established, perfectly proportioned, unperforated, and very beautiful; endowed with all auspicious characteristics, it should consist of seven or five layers.
One should fashion ten gateways starting from the base, well-constructed and well-proportioned;
one should have them made of stone, wood, brick, or as diamond-white palaces.
With plastering and all kinds of perfumes, as well as the splendors of palaces—
such is the fortress of that lord of the earth, endowed with these characteristics.
He protects all the worlds here from fear, together with their treasuries,
even when [the danger] has reached the placement of the lotus, the svastika, the cow-urine, or the *vastu*.
The city or fortress should be constructed with houses situated in the middle of the middle [sections], arranged in rows, and adorned with palaces and dwellings.
Thus ends the seventy-second chapter, titled "The Characteristics of the Gopura Gate," in the glorious Devīpurāṇa.
[Note: The title in the manuscript appears as "gopura-prāra-lakṣaṇam" (ka ga).]
Chapter 73:
The Seventy-third Chapter.
Manu said:
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the construction of lower fortresses (adhodurga),
how and for whom they should be built so as to bring happiness to the world of kings.
In that [place] where the entire universe exists above, difficult to access and mastered by those skilled in fortresses,
one should establish a residence in its lower part, which brings all happiness.
A low-lying site in the east is auspicious, yet it is a fortress for all city-dwellers; however,
if it is low in the southeast, there will be danger from fire, and in the south, fear arising from thieves.
In the south-western direction, the worlds and their inhabitants become destitute;
indeed, they are penniless and bereft of wealth, and other people hold them in contempt.
O child, on the mountain Sannata in the northwest, all the worlds are ever-anxious; but in Durga, which is named after the gentle portion [of the moon], all people are joyful.
O Sage, in the northeast, those dwelling in that fortress situated on low ground become devoted to the Dharma and abound in wealth and grain.
If the eastern part is low, the king shall dwell there below;
if the southeast is low, O Brahmins, it brings both happiness and fear through its fiery energy.
In the south dwell the lowest-born; in the southwest, those who work with weapons;
in the west, water-products and the like, as well as Śūdras and other such people.
In the northwest, people delighting in perfumes and gandharvas shall sound forth;
in the north, there should be a market and water; and in the northeast, the deities and so forth.
If it is otherwise, there is great misfortune; first, it brings an end to the marketplace and the king, O child, but it becomes a source of happiness for those who dwell in its proper location.
A fortress and a city should be constructed, endowed with auspicious features;
one should not allow dwellings dedicated to deities and others to remain empty.
One should not repair a dilapidated house, street, or fortification within the city;
that shall become the king’s share, and one should instead dedicate it to the deities and other such purposes.
And Lord Śaṅkara, accompanied by his attendants and endowed with all auspiciousness, should be fashioned;
in that [temple], all perpetual festivals shall take place, adorned with houses and palaces.
The worlds above shall endure, free from affliction and eternal;
one should not cause them to dwell below in difficult places such as forests and the like.
Dwelling in huts made of grass and other materials, free from fear and the like,
the best of sages should sustain the clouds and other elements with his lower part [of the body].
By upholding [the law], a king incurs great fear arising from his enemies;
neither the kingdom nor the king himself is oppressed by the enemy's forces.
Therefore, for the sake of increasing the strength of the fortress, the practice of living on high is prescribed;
one should dwell well-supported on high, but allow those who are poorly supported to dwell below.
One should not allow intoxicated, insane, or negligent men to dwell in the fortress;
one should not grant authority to a single person, nor to a Śūdra, nor to an actor.
One should not build for a profligate, nor for one who is bound in iron;
one should build a fortress so that it does not crumble like a house struck on the head.
If Śiva is in the northeast and Durgā is below or above, one should press them together;
by the pressure on his own body, the master suffers harm and perishes.
Dwelling in water-born places or mountain fortresses is a perilous abode;
one should especially avoid dwelling permanently in the forest.
One should not make one's dwelling in kingdoms, nor in forests, nor especially in difficult terrains or saline wastelands; likewise, one should not dwell in the wilderness.

In a kingdom, in forests, in wildernesses, in deserts, and likewise in barren lands, there may be a loss of Dharma; furthermore, in the wilderness there is fear born of enemies; therefore, one should abandon dwelling there.
He should live below for the purpose of collecting agricultural products, hides and the like, blood, iron, arrows, machines, medicines, and so forth.
Those dwelling on the merchant streets shall pay grain measured in exchange for gold;
and above that, the king, seeking the welfare of the fortress, shall bring them under his control.
One should always drain the mud, the sputum, and the leaves from difficult depths;
the people living there should always be made strong through service.
In this way, the fortress, well-stocked with wealth and grain, is not depleted;
the people and the treasury increase, and the king prospers in happiness.
Just as the celestial dwellings increased upon the mountain,
so too did the king’s dharma, fame, and glory increase.
Just as there is a duty for embodied beings dwelling in the forest,
so too, by the power of time, may the king’s duty toward his subjects flourish even in times of adversity.
A man-made fortification that is difficult to penetrate should be constructed for a specific purpose and for the sake of victory; listen to me as I explain how this should be done properly.
Having observed that the fortress was well-protected and its strength superior, [he thought:
Water, fuel, grain, fodder, weapons, and so forth.
O mighty-armed one, one should thus fashion an artificial image of the supreme Vijaya.
It may be made of wood, stone, or earth, and likewise constructed with a moat; it should be provided with trees, creepers, and vines, and its interior should be supplied with water.
The outer moat should be well-protected by means of fortifications, siege engines, stones, and the like;
it should be adorned with houses, ramparts, and arched gateways.
It may be joined with a street-filling [structure], or provided with a pavilion;
the pavilion should have one hundred pillars, or twice or thrice that number.
Then, according to the auspicious [measurement], there is a square, a circle, a triangle, and a long crescent moon;
it is enriched with many inner sanctuaries and accompanied by deities and mothers.
One should perform the difficult-to-attain Nāyaka rite, the Nāga-sacrifice accompanied by Umā.
It was filled with many kinds of vessels and the like, and provided with wells and water-stations.
The sun and fire should be given according to the dharma when the recipient is auspicious and free from defects such as being a bow-man (or having a crooked back).
Thus, according to the influence of time, one should construct the great city named Vijaya;
having observed the house and its strength, it should be established according to the rules for low and high positions.
One desiring the fruit of great supernatural power (maharddhi) should construct a fortress with three sets of three inner chambers, distinguished by pillars such as the lunar and others.
One should place the forest in the east and other directions; it has two embryos and twice eight [cells].
Twelve should be assigned on the exterior; therein one should know the strength and weakness.
During entry, cruel planets are givers of fear, while gentle ones bestow gentle fruits; during exit, all are said to be auspicious in the city and the fort.
When planets are situated in their debilitated positions, one such planet causes the destruction of the wife, two cause the loss of friends and wealth, and three cause the death of the eldest son.
One should not undertake the planning of a city or a palace when the Sun is in its sign of debilitation;
the ruler meets with destruction, and that city will never prosper.

A wise person should construct a city for the sake of wealth and victory when the benefic planets are in their exaltations; he should construct a fortress with the malefic planets for the destruction of enemies.
The strength of the Moon, Sun, and Ascendant, the increase of houses, the equal distribution [of points], the lifespan, the givers of fame, the planetary combinations for kingship, and the Aṣṭavarga.
Having understood the strength of the aspect of the Moon, the karma arising from the question,
the portents, and the influence of fate and the nature of beings, one should determine the auspicious and inauspicious regarding the fortress.

The clear Rājayoga, the Samāveśa, and the Saṃvatsaramata, along with the divisions of the [planetary] periods and the reliance on the planets, for the sake of accomplishing the means of ritual action.
The strength known as that of place, time, and nature, as well as that residing in the houses of friends,
and likewise the strength born of rays— these are the foremost among strengths.
One should construct forts, cities, and the like with hundreds of gentle, curved planets;
and those planets shall constantly bestow prosperity upon the master and his people.
When the Drekkāṇa, the Moon, and the lord of the Navāṃśa are auspicious at the time of birth,
as well as the Triṃśāṃśa and Dvādaśāṃśa, one should perform the ritual preparation of the city.
One should recognize a cruel [result] from cruel [planets], and a gentle one is ordained by gentle ones;
O child, this is determined by the aspects [of the planets], excluding those of enemies and friends.
One should not construct a dwelling when the asterisms and the ascendants are past or deficient.

A city or fortress should not be constructed when the moon is in contact with a *kīṭa* asterism, nor when the planets have reached the junctions (*saṃdhyā*), nor when they are situated in the fields of enemies.
With planets that are friendly, endowed with their own strength, well-nourished, aspiring for exaltation,
and situated in their own signs or their own trines, one's undertaking will always be successful.

If difficult points (durgas) are situated nearby, all undertakings will bring auspicious results provided they are occupied by planets born in the friend's trines and endowed with the strength of the Moon.
In the north, there is virtue, wealth, and pleasure; the remaining [planets] come together in that place, bringing fire, burning, fear, loss, affliction from enemies, and constant distress.
One should understand [the deities] beginning with Āgneya for a city where the eastern gate is constructed:
if Īśa is situated in the eastern part, Nanda prospers and Dharma increases.
One obtains all desires by [worshipping] in the east, northeast, and north;
it is auspicious through the presence of rivers in the east and by its essence in the south.
To the west is a pond for libations, and to the north is a blue lotus petal.
Having worshipped Hara, Durgā, the planets, the Mothers, and Vināyaka;
Having offered the bali-oblation according to the procedure prescribed for palaces, construct the city.
Thus ends the seventy-third chapter, titled "The Ritual for Alleviating the Anxiety Concerning the Fortified City," in the Śrī Devīpurāṇa.
%%% Chapter 074.
The seventy-fourth chapter.
Manu said:
Time is eternal, all-pervading, and constant; its state [is determined] by its cause.
Through specific characteristics such as their signs and so forth, they bestow the fruit of merit in the world.

O Sage, the merit known as Saṃkrānti has been previously described; now hear from me about the auspicious Dhārā, the specific fruits for men during eclipses and other occasions, and the various types of holy places (tīrthas).
Gaṅgādvāra, Kurukṣetra, Narmadā, Amarakaṇṭaka,
the holy confluence of the Yamunā, and the Vetravatī together with the Vipāśā.
The Sarayū, the Kauśikī, the Vindhya, the Gaṇḍakī, and the Sarasvatī;
the highly meritorious Candrabhāgā and likewise the river Godāvarī.
The Kāverī, Gomatī, Tāpī, Devikā, Varuṇā,
and others— these most meritorious rivers are proclaimed [to be especially sacred] during eclipses and similar occasions.
And there are many other meritorious [occasions] that grant desires at other times,
as well as those renowned for the solstices (ayana), the equinoxes (viṣuva), and likewise the vyatīpāta yoga.

On the intercalary days, on the new moon, during planetary conjunctions, in times of great delusion, and in public assemblies—on these seven, five, or one lunar mansions [the rites should be performed]. (074.007)
On such festive occasions as these, when the moon is full of all its digits,
on the third lunar day of Vaiśākha, and on the eighth lunar day falling on a Tuesday.
On the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, on a Tuesday, the libation to the ancestors (pitṛ-tarpaṇa) should be performed by the best of men for the fulfillment of all desires.
O Sage, that man who, being devoted, worships Śivāditya on the new moon day or at the transit of the sun, becomes purified; indeed, he becomes utterly pure.
[End of fragment] There is no reference number in the textual portion; please verify it.
O great sage, an eclipse during the month of Kārttika at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā is most excellent; an eclipse in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa at the Devikā is meritorious. (074:011)
In Māgha, the auspicious and holy Narmadā is present;
in Phālguna, she is known as Varūṇā; and in Caitra, she is the holy Sarasvatī.
In Vaiśākha, the Candrabhāgā, the best of rivers, is most meritorious;
in Jyeṣṭha, the Kauśikī is meritorious; and in Āṣāḍha, the Bhāvikā river [is meritorious].
In Śrāvaṇa, the river named Sindhu is best; in Bhādrapada, the Gaṇḍakī is most excellent; in Āśvina, the Sarayū is preeminent; and furthermore, the Narmadā is exceedingly meritorious.
The Godāvarī is greatly meritorious when the moon is joined with Rāhu.
O great sage, when the sun is eclipsed by the moon— that form of darkness—
those who touch the waters of the Narmadā become fulfilled in their purpose.
Those men who touch or bathe in the Vairāja [tirtha] when the sun is eclipsed by Rāhu are not ordinary mortals.
By bathing there, one obtains the fruit of a royal sacrifice; by seeing it, the fruit born of the gift of a cow;
by touching it, a result equal to the Gomedha sacrifice; and by drinking [the water], one obtains the Sautrāmaṇi.
Having bathed, one shall undoubtedly attain the merit of the Vājimedha sacrifice.
During an eclipse of the sun or the moon, as well as during the northern solstice, the Gaṅgā is to be viewed in this way; likewise is the goddess Sarasvatī.
Whatever fruit is proclaimed for the Maṇḍala of Śivāditya, a person shall obtain that very same fruit when there is a conjunction with Mars during a planetary eclipse.
Whatever merit is proclaimed to be found in saline wastes or in forest lands,
that is even greater here during an eclipse due to the greatness of the time.
Or whoever, having brought water, performs an ablution according to the rite with pure water accompanied by mantras— the merit of that person is even greater than the former.
O Brahmin, according to one's own means, by means of vessels made of metal, earth, wood, or stone, one obtains blameless fruit.
Or those best of men, O Sage, who, having risen every morning, fetch earth from that sacred ford and pay their respects to it; ||074:024a-d||
They all become liberated from evil, free from disease.
O Brahmin, he who, having bathed there, worships Raviśvara with offerings of fruits and flowers shall become free from all affliction.
Having bathed according to the prescribed rite with water purified by mantras from jars filled with flowers, fruits, and other auspicious items, he shall obtain all his desires.
Whatever merit has been thus described by me, as heard from the mouth of Brahmā, may all of that belong to him in the forests and in the saline wastes.
I shall describe the forests, as well as the saline wastes: Saindhava, the Daṇḍaka forest, Naimiṣa, and Kurujāṅgala.
Upalāvṛta, Āraṇya, Jambūmārga, Puṣkara,
and Himavāsa— these are proclaimed as the five most excellent forests.
Whoever should renounce their life-breaths in these nine forests,
becoming a guest in the world of Brahmā, goes to the supreme state.
O Śivā, the fruit that is obtained at Kālañjara and Mahākāla, as well as at Karṇikā, Śivākhya, Kālikā, and Gaṇaya, is equal in all these sacred sites.

Thus ends the seventy-fourth chapter, titled "Praise of Eclipse-Sites, Rivers, Forests, and Saline Grounds," in the glorious Devīpurāṇa. [Regarding the Praise of Eclipse-Sites, Rivers, Forests, and Saline Grounds.]
Chapter Seventy-Five:
On the Himavat, Hemakūṭa, Vindhya, and Mahendra mountains.
To King Mahāsena at Vaidiśa or Ujjayinī.
O Sage, whether at the highly meritorious Gopagiri, or at Citrakūṭa, or at Kālañjara, or at Kāśī, or at the mountain named Puṣpa-veda; ||075:002||
Then one should cause [the gift] to be given to Maheśvara in Ujjayinī or Ayodhyā;
in these meritorious regions, at the conjunction of the equinoxes and solstices.
O child, at Puṣkara, Naimiṣa, Pañcamukha, and Akṣaya,
as well as on the mountain, by the gift of a water-stream, affliction from the planets does not arise.
When the body has reached many crooked states, there shall be no fear, just as for a calf;
or the affliction of the birth star and the star of conception is warded off by the bestowed stream.
O great sage, at Vahnikāga on the path of Jambū, worship is always performed; the descent of the stream (Dhārāpāta) is especially distinguished there, and one attains all desires on the Narmadā.
By offering libations according to the prescribed rite into the Gaṅgā, the Kālindī, and the great lake, no fear arises anywhere.
It dispels the affliction caused by Saturn and the Sun, as well as that caused by Jupiter and Mars,
which arises every year, through worship performed according to the prescribed rite.
O child, one should ward off the affliction arising from the planets during the year through the constant recitation of mantras; O child, no fear exists anywhere.
In a secluded place, free from the wicked and devoid of evil beings,
one who desires prosperity should perform the continuous fire sacrifice (dhārā-homa) as prescribed.
One should cause the stream to fall upon the tongue— neither too fast nor too slow—
regulated with a vigilant mind by one who has conquered death.
Success arising from mantra-yoga accomplishes both the seen and the unseen;
the worship of the planets removes even the threefold suffering that has arisen.
The planets are said to be of three kinds, and their mantras are likewise considered to be of three types:
those born from the limbs (aṅgaja), the root-mantras (mūlamantra), and the piṇḍas consisting of words (padagata).
They should be employed at the time of the fire-oblation (homa) and likewise at the time of worship;
in this way, one attains accomplishment pertaining to both this world and the heavenly realms.
O Sage, through the application of activity at the time of cultivation, it is attained within the stream.
A continuous stream of offerings should be made using mechanical devices, vessels, jars, and so forth;

with the weight of your hair laid down in loose tresses, braids, and open curls?"
The abodes of their ornaments— garlands of flowers smeared with sandalwood paste— shone as they trailed behind them, suspended from their heads with their sharp tips hanging down.
It shines with the distinction of its branches and leaves, with a tilaka-mark upon its forehead, and with another particular feature: the rising sun.
Another shone with earrings set with gems and leaves,
appearing like frightened young deer with their long, white and black stripes.
In the city of Śrī Hāṭakeśvara, their eyes shine forth;
O Smara, [dwell there] forever with such women who constantly afflict you with passion.
They discern and delight in the enjoyments of pleasure; fully satisfied, they are permeated by auspiciousness.
Thus ends the eighty-second chapter, titled "Description of the City of Hāṭakeśvara," in the glorious Devīpurāṇa.

Chapter 89: The Eighty-Ninth Discourse.
Śakra said: O Goddess, I wish to hear that means by which you bestow all fruits upon everyone, as well as the fruit associated with the ninth day.
"Tell me, O Brahmā, does the fruit reside in the self?
Brahmā replied:
"Whether in the month of Āśvina, or Māgha, or Caitra, or even Śrāvaṇa..."
O Hari, the vow should be undertaken starting from the dark fortnight and increasing during the bright fortnight.
On the eighth day of the dark fortnight of Āśvina, one should perform the rite with a single meal,
honoring the Goddess in the form of Maṅgalā or as the slayer of Ruru.
One should worship with ninefold offerings of perfumes, garlands, and food presentations; O child, one should feed young maidens and those men who are devotees of the Goddess.
On the ninth day, one should perform the human sacrifice and the nocturnal rite; one should pass the tenth day without food.
On the eleventh day, there should again be a fast; such is the procedure.
O Śakra, one should observe the fast according to the prescribed rule until the eighth day of the bright fortnight;
every day there should be bathing, fire-offerings, recitation, worship, and the feeding of virgins.
This should be performed by a pair of twice-born men who are devoted to the Goddess;
on the ninth day, the slaughter of animals such as buffaloes, goats, and sheep [is to be carried out].
O Bhūta and Vetāla, this must be performed by a multitude of twice-born ones who have realized the truth, and not according to one's own personal desire.
There, the twice-born men, devoted to the Goddess, brought adorned maidens.
In that regard, the unconditioned [is attained] through watching actors and dancers, through chariot processions and keeping vigils;
one should give gifts according to one's ability with devotion toward all beings. (089.009)
Men who possess the form of Mahābhairava and wear garlands of bones should be especially honored when they are adorned with beautiful garments and ornaments.
O best of gods, Śakra, it should be performed for the attainment of all desired objects; by this rite, one obtains the fruit according to one's wish.
Maṅgalā, Bhairavī, Durgā, Vārāhī, Tridaśeśvarī,
Umā, Haimavatī, Kanyā, Kapālī, and Kaiṭabheśvarī.
A person should recite the names Kālī, Brāhmī, Māheśī, Kaumārī, Madhusūdanī, Vārāhī, Vāsavī, and Carccā, as well as other names.
One should honor and feed the maidens according to the rites prescribed in the scriptures,
[providing] garments, ornaments, girdles, bracelets, and waist-bands.
Those seeking happiness should give according to their own capacity, being devoted to the Goddess,
for nine nights, or seven, five, three, or one.
O Śakra, one should pass the month of Āśvina by eating only once a day, by eating only at night, by not begging for food, and by fasting, until the eighth day of the bright fortnight.
One should worship Maṅgalā there in the mandala prepared according to the ritual rules,
which is endowed with all true existence and which effects every rite.
O Śakra, bestower of all desires, one shall obtain all desires;
for one desiring wealth, it grants wealth, and for one desiring a kingdom, it grants a kingdom.
O son, this bestows health, O child, and destroys great sins;
it should be performed by all castes—by men, women, children, and eunuchs alike.
O Śakra, because this goddess is omnipresent, eternal, and yields great fruit, she grants [her rewards],
my son, through this rite without hesitation.
The great fruit of all vows, which is the source of all vows,
the highly meritorious one known as the Ninth, has been fully revealed to you.
This [teaching on yoga] must not be told to one who lacks devotion, to a fool, or to one who argues without reason;
it should be given to one who is devoted, peaceful, and intent upon Śiva and Viṣṇu.
Even for one devoid of devotion and liberation, a man who is a devotee of the Goddess, of virtuous conduct, and intent on the worship of the maiden,
obtains all his desires in this very world without a doubt.
For him there shall be no mental anxieties nor physical ailments, nor shall there be fear of enemies;
he shall always achieve victory in battle, even if he is alone.
By hearing it, one obtains all desires without the need for deliberation.
Thus ends the eighty-ninth chapter, titled "The Vow of the Eighth and Ninth Days," in the glorious Devīpurāṇa. [Variant titles:
The Vow of the Eighth and Ninth Days (ka); The Vow of the Auspicious Eighth Day (ga).]

Chapter 090: The Chapter on the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī’s Questions Regarding the Dharma-Door of the Non-Arising of All Phenomena and the Attainment of the Seal of the Tathāgata’s Samādhi of the Non-Arising of All Phenomena. Part One. At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the great assembly: “Good sons, in the past, immeasurable, boundless, inconceivable, and incalculable eons ago, there was a Buddha named King of the Radiance of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksambuddha, Vidyācaraṇasampanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddho Bhagavān. That Buddha, the World-Honored One, appeared in the world during the auspicious kalpa of the Auspicious Eon. His land was called Pure and Adorned with All Jewels. That land was level and smooth, without unevenness, thorns, or pits; it was free from mountains, rivers, and marshes, and was adorned with various precious trees. Its ground was composed of lapis lazuli, and it was strewn with golden sand. It was filled with celestial flowers and perfumed with divine incense. There were no hells, animals, or hungry ghosts; nor were there the realms of asuras or other evil paths. Its people lived for eighty-four thousand great kalpas, and all were born spontaneously by transformation. They were adorned with the thirty-two marks of a great man and possessed the eight emancipations. Their minds were pure and free from affliction, and they were able to fly through the air. They had no parents, wives, children, or kinsmen; they did not engage in buying or selling, nor did they possess wealth or property. They were free from the three poisons and the five desires, and their minds were always joyful and at ease. That Buddha, the World-Honored One, preached the Dharma for the sake of his disciples, and after ninety-two hundred million great kalpas, he entered parinirvāṇa. After his parinirvāṇa, the True Dharma remained for eighty-four thousand great kalpas, and the Semblance Dharma remained for eighty-four thousand great kalpas. During the period of the Semblance Dharma, there was a king named Universal Light. He governed the four continents and possessed the seven treasures and the thousand sons. He ruled according to the Dharma, bringing peace and security to the world. At that time, there was a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva named Mañjuśrī, who, out of compassion for sentient beings, traveled throughout the ten directions to preach the Dharma. He went to the palace of King Universal Light and sat upon a jeweled throne. At that time, King Universal Light, seeing the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, rose from his seat, joined his palms, and paid homage to him. He then asked Mañjuśrī: ‘World-Honored One, what is the Dharma-door for attaining the seal of the Tathāgata’s samādhi of the non-arising of all phenomena? Mañjuśrī replied: ‘Great King, if one can contemplate all phenomena as being like empty space—neither arising nor ceasing, neither coming nor going, neither permanent nor impermanent, neither self nor non-self, neither existent nor non-existent, neither real nor unreal, neither true nor false, neither defiled nor pure, neither increasing nor decreasing, neither born nor dying, neither beginning nor end, neither cause nor effect, neither agent nor recipient, neither subject nor object, neither grasping nor abandoning, neither form nor mind, neither internal nor external, neither within nor without, neither in the past, present, nor future, neither in this world nor in another world, neither in the realm of desire, form, nor formlessness, neither in saṃsāra nor nirvāṇa—if one can contemplate all phenomena in this way, one will attain the seal of the Tathāgata’s samādhi of the non-arising of all phenomena. At that time, King Universal Light, having heard these words, was overjoyed and said: ‘Excellent, World-Honored One! I shall now practice according to these instructions. Having spoken thus, he immediately offered his kingdom, his seven treasures, his thousand sons, and his entire retinue to the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, saying: ‘I offer all these to you, World-Honored One, to serve as

The gift of land, the gift of cows, gold, clothing, sesame seeds, water,

Those who understand the reality of knowledge and inquiry, even while enjoying the pleasures of a king who treads the path of the righteous, attain the supreme goal.

One kills an elephant with a grain of barley and a horse with a mustard seed;

For knowledge indeed disregards family, birth, form, or personal worth;

Knowledge alone resides in the hearts of all the elderly, for respect is due to the elder;

[With actors, bards,
and dancers,] in a secluded place and under an auspicious constellation, it should be performed daily with confidence according to this rite, on a day with a favorable asterism and a propitious date.

In that manner, one should place it in a book or on cloth, worshipped according to the prescribed rite; having done so, one should likewise meditate upon the Mothers, [thinking]: "May they be dear to me."

To one who is constantly engaged in study, who delights in the gift of knowledge,

If one should bestow the Yoga-śāstra through the power of the gift of knowledge, that learned person is born into a family endowed with all enjoyments.

Chapter Ninety-Two.
Śakra said:

"O child, that which is called Cārcikā—the supreme wealth of Dhanasampadā—is the most excellent among vows; it crosses over even the most terrible [obstacles], being half a month in duration, or even a quarter. [099:045]
Or else, one should perform it for a month beginning with Śrāvaṇa in due order;
for, O child, this is not attained by men lacking merit, nor even by the best of kings.
But he with whom Nandinī is pleased attains the state of the Blessed Goddess.
"Bhavatī-bhāvā Kha, Bhagavatī-bhāvā Ka.

Chapter One Hundred:
The Hundredth Discourse.
Agastya said:
Of all vessels indeed, the goddess Śaṅkarī is the supreme vessel;
worship her, for she is the knowledge that bestows both seen and unseen rewards. 100:001.
O Śakra, this rule of the Brahma-śāstra has been declared as bringing victory; O dear one, the full moon day of Śrāvaṇa is called Śakrī and is a bearer of auspiciousness.
Śakra said:
"That which is proclaimed as Vijayā leads to the accomplishment of all desires."
O best of gods, I desire to hear that [account] in its true essence.
Brahmā said:
For the sake of sons, for the sake of sovereignty and learning, or even for fame and good fortune;
and for one desiring victory and health, one should observe the Vijayā full moon.
On the full moon day,
he should fashion an image endowed with all the auspicious marks, using either gold, silver, or even alms-food, as well as a sword and sandals. ||100:005||
Taking her under an auspicious constellation, adorned with white garments, provided with sprouts of barley and śāli rice, and decorated with a parasol; ||100:006||

One should offer fruits for the sake of the fruit [of one's desires], barley sprouts for the sake of victory,
flowers for one desiring good fortune, and jewels for the sake of long life and wealth.
For the destruction of enemies, for the desire of what is dear,
and for the fulfillment of all purposes and desires, you should cause food to be given according to one's means.
Then, as if receiving the requested Vidyā, one should ask the Goddess for forgiveness;
for the sake of a son, one should feed children, and for the sake of victory, one should feed women and twice-born men.
And in the house,
one should feed those who seek the Dharma and wealth with food consecrated by this vidyā;
and one should give a sacrificial fee to the preceptor and teacher, as well as to the maidens and the brahmins.
One should cause [the gift] to be given according to one's ability, having thus favored him;
one who desires a son should partake of the finest food from the village consecrated with the vidyā-mantra.
One should eat from a separate vessel and must not cause distress; according to this procedure, the mantra for this very purpose is as follows: ||100:017||
[With the son's blood], let him who has devoured me here bestow that seed upon the earth;

Oṃ, homage to the Blessed One whose semen is undiminished; svāhā!
At the time of sexual union, one should indeed contemplate the deity who is the Lord of the Thirty-three,

Oṃ, to Retā, to Mahāretā, to Sarvavīrya, to Mahābala, to Kāma, to Kāmadeva: grant me my desires—ṭhaṃ ṭhaṃ!
O Great Ascetic, one should resort to a bed consecrated with this mantra;
it bestows eight sons, provided that one does not fall into delusion.
Having thus received the vidyā, one should worship the goddess constantly.
It brings about the attainment of all desired goals, even those previously unattained;
for whatever fruits and flowers arise here during the rainy season, [they are all achieved].
O child, one should cause [the deity] to go here; for a Brahmin, a daughter, or even a teacher, one should cause [an offering] to be given.
O dear one, according to what is available, that which has been heard, flowers, and fruits should be offered.
Whether it be the ninth day of the month of Śrāvaṇa, Āśvina, or Kārtika,
one who desires success must certainly abide by this rule.
Through burnt offerings, the observance of vows, and the propitiation of the *caru* and mantras,
one who is childless obtains a son, wealth, good fortune, and long life.
Alternatively, by this knowledge, she is characterized as vast and white,
due to the teaching on the *rājapūraka* and the *vaṭa-śṛṅga* mantras.

At the end of that, one obtains the fruit of *nāgakeśara* flowers;
through the gift of clarified butter and water, one attains the fruit by means of knowledge. 100.028.
O Ga, he becomes a world-conqueror, a lord of the earth and a master of vidyās.
Thus has this entire supreme vow called Vijaya been explained to you. 100.29
It bestows success upon all people through the practice of austerity according to the prescribed rule.

Chapter One Hundred and One: Ekādhikaśatatamo'dhyāyaḥ.
Manu said:
Hereafter, O child, I shall proclaim that which brings about beauty and good fortune, by means of which Śaṅkarī is pleased according to the rite of the lunar mansions (nakṣatra).

Beginning from the *mārga* [root] and proceeding to the *mūla*, one who observes a fast should worship the feet with garlands made of jasmine (*jāti*). The breaking of the fast (*pāraṇa*) should be performed according to the lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*) specified.
Beginning with the month of Māgha,
one should worship the two shanks of Brahmā with *gayavānna* prepared with sacrificial oblation (*havis*);
and with *kahlāra* lotuses and *mṛgarāja* flowers, one should partake of a meal of sesame and black gram.
Therefore, O Brahmins, one should first worship the knees during the Aśvinī asterism with jasmine and black flowers; the food offering should consist of curd and sugar.
During both Āṣāḍhas, one should worship that Goddess with bilva leaves;
at the end of the lunar mansion, one should eat, and that constitutes the breaking of the fast (pāraṇa). ||101:005||
One should worship her who brings to completion the beautiful pair of breasts on the form, as well as the secret Phālguna;
one should offer curd-rice as the food offering and perform ten million sacrifices with *kṛtika* flowers.
One should worship Uṣā and Nityā at the edge of the flower-grove; one should offer *gadamana* and white flowers, and sweetmeats (*laḍḍūkā*) for the Goddess’s meal.
In the month of Bhādrapada, one should worship the two flanking deities with white flowers.
The milk-rice is the meal for the Brahmins at the end of the lunar mansion;
on the day of Puṣya, one should worship the Goddess residing in the womb with garlands of mango blossoms.
Under Anurādhā, one should worship the chest with offerings of curd, *kāga* (goat), ghee, and black gram rice;
one should offer garlands of yellow *karṇikāra* flowers and food cooked in ghee. ||101:009||
One should worship the back of the sky with golden flowers during the asterism Dhaniṣṭhā, offering food mixed with milk and rice;
one should also worship the Goddess in the branches, offering ear-ornaments as an oblation.
Fragrant milk-rice (pāyasa) should be offered as food upon lotus leaves;
furthermore, the hands should be honored with the hand using substances such as uśīra and tagara.
On the Punarvasu nakṣatra, one should offer molasses and milk as the food offering (naivedya) and worship Mañjulā with saffron; furthermore, sixty-day rice (ṣaṣṭhika) should be given as food.
One should worship the fingers with *naravān*, *bhujaṅga*, and *daivatyai*, as well as with the *punnāga* and other flowers;
food and water should be offered after purification, and one should worship the neck with the *jyeṣṭhā* stars.
Food, ghee, and other offerings should be given to the Goddess with white garlands;
one should worship her with red flower petals and ears, and feed her sacrificial oblations (havis).
In the month of Puṣya, one should consume rice mixed with sugar along with lotuses and other offerings;
in Svāti, the teeth should be cleaned, and one should worship with deep red buds.
One should worship Śatabhiṣaj with jasmine, nāgakeśara, and sandalwood;
one should offer dates and sugar as food, and one should worship Maghā in the nostrils.
Likewise, food prepared from wheat should be offered with barley flowers;
one should worship the goddess Mṛganetrī with fragrant blossoms.

One should worship the forehead of the Goddess with variegated and multicolored garlands, her face with variegated food offerings, and her head with *bharaṇī* flowers and garlands of *campaka* and other blossoms.
One should offer a meal of milk-rice and worship those with moist hair;
one should worship the Goddess with jasmine and other flowers, and offer a meal to the Soul of All.
Indeed, these are the Mothers of the Constellations; therefore, those who desire beautiful sons should always offer oblations of ghee and gifts of food to Śambhu or Viṣṇu. (101.20)

A pair of garments should be given to a brahmin who has conquered his senses, who is accompanied by his wife, who is skilled in the meaning of the Goddess’s scriptures, and who is proficient in the knowledge of Śiva. 101.021.
Her face is like the full moon, her eyes are as long as lotus petals;
her teeth are beautiful and white, and her ears are well-fleshed.
Her hair resembled the bellies of bees, her voice was like the song of the cuckoo;
she had copper-colored lips, eyes like lotus petals, beautiful hands, and was bent by the weight of her breasts.
Her navel was spiraling to the right, her thighs resembled the petals of a plantain tree,
she possessed beautiful hips and a soft waist, and she was adorned with lovely, well-knit fingers. ||101:024||
The woman was beautiful, and her husband was a man of great arms, with a broad chest and wide frame, his face resembling the full moon. (101.025)
With white teeth and the gait of an elephant, possessing great strength and prowess,
beloved by all the world, and with eyes as long as lotus petals.
By this vow, one becomes a great brahmin who is gentle in speech, endowed with a pleasant countenance, captivating to women, and equal to the god of love. (101.027)
The knower of the meaning of all scriptures, the union with women, the attainment of desired objects, the auspicious arrival of fortune,
that which is called the Great Puṣya asterism, and the best among vows— [these are found here]. (101.028)

O best of sages, even in times of adversity, one should not create division with those who are dear; nor, O most excellent of munis, should one abandon even those things that appear to be of a faulty nature.
Thus ends the one hundred and first chapter, titled "The Nakṣatra Vow," in the Śrī Devīpurāṇa.
[In the first incarnation of the Goddess, the Nakṣatra Vow.
Chapter 102:
The One Hundred and Second Chapter.
Agastya said:
He who gives a water-cow in Āṣāḍha, likewise ghee in Bhādrapada,
and sesame-cows in Māgha, obtains benefit by having given them.
The Vidyādhara said:
O best of sages, what gifts should be given to the Goddess?
Tell me what vessels, what place, what time, and what ritual procedure [are required].
"I wish to hear about those; please tell me out of your grace.
Agastya said:
"O best of kings, even those vegetables which were obtained by him through righteous means—"
The dwellings of the goddess, of her maidens, and of the women were always frequented by Brahmins devoted to her and by others as well, at all times. (102.004)
Especially during the rainy season, O child, the Goddess grants all desires;
[one should visit] the region of Nandā, Gayā, and the mountain, as well as the Gaṅgā, Narmadā, and Puṣkara.
Vārāṇasī, Kurukṣetra, Prayāga, Jambukeśvara,
Kedāra, Bhīmanāda, Daṇḍaka, and the place called Puṣkara.
[The Bhīmadāna and] Someśvara, which is of great merit, as well as Amarakaṇṭaka; likewise Kālañjara and Vindhya, where Guha indeed has his dwelling. 102:007.
[The gift of] a cow and its calf, wealth, land, gold, grain, sesame, clothing, ghee, and so forth;
according to the prescribed rite, by means of fasting, eating only one meal, or eating only at night. ||102:008||
One who is pure, purified in heart, and endowed with patience, truthfulness, vows, and so forth, shall deliver even a donor as small as a mustard seed by giving it. (102:009)
Furthermore, O child, he who, according to the prescribed rite during the rainy season, bestows sesame seeds and other offerings upon Brahmins and Brahmin maidens for the sake of the Goddess—
Then the Goddess is quickly satisfied by means of the vidyā;
hereafter I shall proclaim the supreme vow of the goddess Nandā.
O child, one who is purified should, according to their ability, fashion a pair of sandals made of gold, by which they will soon be well-pleased by the high-souled ones.
Having performed the fire sacrifice with mango, dūrvā grass, unbroken rice, and bilva leaves,
and having worshipped the Goddess within— that which has been consecrated— either upon a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) or in images; 102:013.
One should also offer it to a Brahmin devoted to Him and present it before virgins;
such a person is liberated from all sins and goes to the heavenly world.
Upon the dissolution of the body, the one of great wisdom shall become a lord of the Vidyādharas;
and in due time, having returned here to this earth, he shall become the best of kings.
There is no doubt that this was spoken by Brahmā to Prajāpati, Vasiṣṭha, Kaśyapa, and Dakṣa. (102:016)
In the same way, O Indra among kings, you too should perform this Padavrata,
if you desire great sovereignty and wish to bring the Goddess into your direct perception.
Thus ends the one hundred and second chapter, titled "The Padavrata," in the Śrī Devīpurāṇa.
[End of the Padavrata in the first incarnation of the Goddess.]
Chapter 103:
The One Hundred and Third Chapter.
Agastya said: Now, therefore, I shall fully describe to you that unsurpassed gift by which,
in ancient times, the Goddess was pleased with the high-souled Śakra.
O King, for Śukra, one should obtain a cow that is blue, white, pale-red, tawny, or even black; one that is easy to milk, has a calf of suitable age, and yields milk without difficulty. (103.2)
Having taken [the image], one should worship the Goddess according to the rules with garlands and lotuses,
and with incense consisting of the five exudations, along with turuṣka, aguru, and sandalwood.
Having offered the mantra-worship, one should present an offering of food (naivedya) to the Goddess;
it should consist of milk-rice mixed with ghee, and one should likewise ask her for forgiveness.
One should offer a milch cow along with her calf, accompanied by gold, clothing, and a girdle, to a twice-born man who is a devotee of Śiva; thus one shall obtain great merit. ||103:005||
For as many hairs as there are on his body, for that many years shall he dwell in the city of the Goddess;
here, freed from sin, he is born as an excellent king.
Having performed this rite, Manu attained the unsurpassed world;
O King, listen as I describe it to you according to the prescribed rule. (103:007)
One should have a cow made of gold from the auspicious banks of the Yamunā, with silver hooves;
having clothed it in garments, one should worship that destroyer of the sons of Danu.
With various colorful flowers, and with offerings of perfumes and incense,
one should likewise ask the Goddess for forgiveness and bring that cow to that very place.
O Goddess, by your command, this [gift] is bestowed upon your devotees;
furthermore, you should cause it to be given to the king of Brahmins, who is permeated by the spirit of Śiva.
Desiring imperishable fruits for the sake of purification through atonement,
Manu as well as other supreme kings observed this vow.
Having concentrated his mind, he attains that which is like nectar;
O child, having rescued seven preceding and seven succeeding generations even if they were established in sin, he leads them to the unsurpassed world of the goddesses.
[sa-tu-kha, sa-tya-ka] Thus ends the one hundred and third chapter, titled "The Hemagovrata," in the Śrī Devīpurāṇa.

The One Hundred and Fourth Chapter.
Manu said: One should give the best of juices in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa; ghee in Pauṣa yields great fruit; sesame seeds in Māgha, O best of sages; and grains in Phālguna. (104:001)
In the month of Caitra, the best of the twice-born should give various garments and diverse ornaments;

Sandalwood should be given in the month of Āṣāḍha, and camphor yields great fruit; fresh butter is considered appropriate in the month of Nabhas, and in Caitra and Proṣṭhapada as well.
O Sage, he who offers molasses, sugar, sugarcane, and other sweets such as *laḍḍūkas* during the month of Aśvina, and who bestows the gift of lamps in Kārttika, gains great merit. (104.004)
One obtains all desires in due order from the path thus described;
one should give a cow made of ghee in the month of Pauṣa, and likewise one made of sesame seeds in Māgha.
In the month of Jyeṣṭha, one should give a cow consisting of water with a calf made of ghee, which yields great fruit;
in Śrāvaṇa, one should give a beautiful cow that bestows great rewards.
[One should give] a cow that has died after giving birth, described as having horns made entirely of gold, feet of silver,
a bell-metal vessel, accompanied by a bell, and adorned with small tinkling bells. ||104:007||
O child, a cow with a calf and a rope should be given according to this rite,
[dedicating it] to the Goddess, Brahmā, Īśa, Sūrya, or Viṣṇu, as prescribed by rule.
O best of the twice-born, having worshipped with a mind perfected in its own nature,
one should give to one who is free from passion and devoid of desire and anger. (104:009)

One who possesses a pure disposition and wealth, and who bestows cows upon those who do not beg, who are of good conduct, disciplined, and observant of vows, shall obtain delightful desires in the heavenly world. (104:010)
Agastya said:
I shall describe the sesame-cow by which Durgā is pleased;
by giving her away, even one who has performed evil deeds becomes stainless.
Hear now, O best of kings, that goddess who brings about sovereignty, sons, and divine fortune, and who becomes manifest to you in no time at all.
Having obtained permission from the god and his goddess, and having bathed with his senses subdued,
he should worship them with flowers, perfumes, food, incense, lamps, and sacred purifiers.
Having offered various oblations into the fire, O child, fashion an image of the Goddess made of *droṇa* measures, adorned with all kinds of jewels, using one *āḍhaka*.
One should fashion a cow with golden horns and silver hooves, beautiful and possessing a sense of smell through perfumes;
its mouth should be made of molasses, and likewise its tongue of food.
The blanket should be made of white thread, its legs likewise made of sugarcane;
its back should be of copper, and its eyes set with gems and pearls.
With a fine thread, beautiful leaf-shaped earrings, and auspicious teeth made of fruit, one should fashion breasts of fresh butter; make it a garland of flowers. (104.017)
One should offer a pure vessel adorned with pearls and gems and filled with fruits,
covered with a pair of auspicious cloths and decorated with a beautiful parasol.
Having fashioned [the image] endowed with such a form, one possessed of faith should offer a bell-metal milking vessel, saying: "May the Goddess be pleased with me."
Having consecrated it with mantras, one should present it to a devotee of that [deity].
As many sesame seeds, garments, minerals, roots, and fruits as there may be—
A man shall dwell in heaven for as many years as there are particles of dust on the earth,
having rendered his ancestors free from sin, even though they have gone to the lower realms.
Having reached the auspicious world of the Goddess, even one who has followed the path of a cow shall establish himself there without hesitation;
there, my child, I delight with him as long as the moon and stars endure. (104.022)
Likewise, one who has come here from Kālādihā is born as a lord of the earth, endowed with discipline and splendor, possessing many sons, and filled with happiness. ||104:023||
Furthermore, O Goddess, by being free from enmity and by constantly performing worship according to the rules,
one attains the great sovereignty of yoga and reaches the imperishable state. ||104:024||
[End of] the one hundred and fourth chapter, titled "The Cow of Sesame," in the glorious *Devīpurāṇa*.

Chapter 105: The One Hundred and Fifth Chapter.
Agastya said:
In the absence of sesame seeds, a wise man should offer a cow made of clarified butter;
having bathed Bhavānī with ghee and milk according to the prescribed rite.
One should worship with garlands, wreaths, and most delightful food offerings;
one should bring all the necessary materials and prepare them there.
In a jar of cow’s ghee, adorned with garlands of flowers,
the wise man should likewise cover a bronze vessel with cloths.
One should fashion the pedestals from gold, along with gems, corals, and pearls; likewise, one should make the hooves out of silver.
Likewise, golden eyes and two auspicious horns made of black agallochum [should be placed];
seven kinds of grain at its side, and a woolen blanket made of silk-cloth.
The two ears should be made of the seven grains, the nose of tagara and camphor, and the breasts auspiciously fashioned from fruit;
the face should be smeared with ghee and milk, and one should fashion the tongue from sugar.
The tail should be made of linen cloth, its hairs from white mustard seeds;
the back should be copper-colored and variegated, beautiful in its oily appearance.
One should fashion a cow with a calf made of ghee, endowed with all the auspicious marks;
having thus prepared these two, one should worship Nandā according to the prescribed rite.

This jewel of clarified butter should be given to one who is devoted to it and has mastered the auspicious scriptures; take it for my benefit and as a favor to my mother, who is ever helpful. (105.009)
"May Queen Nandinī, Maṅgalā, Carcikā, and Umā be pleased for the sake of the mind's benefit.
Having spoken thus, one should worship the cow, making her joyful and compliant with the mind. (105.010)
According to this procedure, a cow fashioned from barley, śāli rice, or sugarcane should be given; or else, a cow made of gold, jewels, food, or cloth should be given according to this rite.
One is liberated from all sins and shall attain all desires;
there, rivers flow with milk and lakes flow with clarified butter.
In that world where the mud is made of milk, he is glorified;
endowed with supreme joy, he attains lordship over them.
O dear one, from the eastern and western directions, twenty-one [breaths] belong to the self;
furthermore, having arrived here in this world, the earth reaches a hundred [years].
Ten times ten million [worlds] are situated there in space;
this is the fruition for those with desires, as it has been described.
One who gives a cow of ghee, being free from desire, attains the world of the Goddess. (105.015)

Kha] Thus ends the one hundred and fifth chapter, titled "The Ghee Cows," in the Śrī Devīpurāṇa.

Chapter 106:
The One Hundred and Sixth Chapter.
Agastya said:
Listen, O child, to how the Goddess is propitiated by the water-cow:
a jar completely filled with water, accompanied by a pair of garments and gems.
In this regard, O dear one, [it should be] joined with the pair [of syllables], endowed with all the seed-syllables, and beautified with sprouts of *dūrvā* grass;
as well as with *murā*, young *uśīra*, *kuṣṭha*, *āmalaka*, and sandalwood.
One should prepare the ritual arrangement consisting of a garland, an umbrella, sandals, and four vessels of sesame seeds,
along with a vessel containing curd, honey, and ghee.
O dear one, the wise man, having fasted or eaten only at night, should worship Vatsaka made of sacrificial oblations according to the prescribed rite after duly worshipping the Goddess Ambā. 106:004.
One should give [this] to a devotee of the Goddess; he shall obtain all his desires.
The Goddess Jayā is the slayer of enemies and the destroyer of the fear of the gods.
Salutations to the Mother of the Vedas, the excellent Durgā, who moves everywhere and bestows auspiciousness.
O dear one, with this mantra, one should consecrate that gift for the purpose of giving:

*kha*]— thus ends the one hundred and sixth chapter, titled "The Water-Cows," in the venerable *Devīpurāṇa*.

Chapter 107:
The One Hundred and Seventh Chapter.
Manu said:
"This Blessed One is the Self-Existent; he was sung of by you in the past as the source of the Vedas.
From Śiva down to the sages, those who follow the Smṛtis are the ones who establish the [sacred] sites."
[O wise ones, you are the agents: How could the Goddess be my mother? This is my curiosity. (107:002)
[Mātā ka ga] Brahmā said:
Knowledge, power, and action are proclaimed to be the forms of the Goddess as cows.
The Mātṛkā is indeed the power of knowledge (jñāna-śakti), while that which has the form of darkness (tamas) is the power of action (kriyā-śakti).
That [power], beginning with Vāmā, becomes threefold as Jyeṣṭhā and Raudrī, remaining straight;
she is Kuṇḍalinī, shaped like a triple-folded coil, and endowed with two dots at each of the two [ends].
She gave birth to the eight groups of sounds, O Vasu; these were further divided into two types:
the nasalized and the voiced, totaling ninety-nine afflicted [phonemes].
His first [form], Śiva, should be seen as situated in the group of the Mother;
divided at the end of the sixteen, he is established within the letter *a*.
In the syllable *A*, some [beings] abide in the form of Brahmā and others in the form of Śiva; Viṣṇu, Skanda, Yama, Śakra, and Carcikā likewise reside within it.
In the letter *ka*, within the *ka-vindu*, there are indeed the moon and the sun; thereafter, she is considered to be hundredfold.
Listen to you how the Goddess, the Mother of the Vedas, becomes the embodiment of action (*kriyā*). ||107:008||
In the Bindu are the fires and suns;
the syllable Om, the Praṇava, the Vedas, and the Gāyatrī born from the reed—
these are declared to be the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga), while the other four are the secondary limbs (upāṅga).

Vasiṣṭha said:
The Mothers [worship] Bhairava and Durgā, who has taken refuge in a dilapidated house.
But that best of the twice-born who, having renovated the palace, should cause it to be built anew; ||118:001||
Whether it be made of baked brick, wood, or stone— listen, O best of the twice-born, to the fruit of worship performed there for Brahmā, Indra, Rudra, Viṣṇu, and the Sun.
The unsurpassed ritual of merit is praised as the path for the Mothers, and there is no fear of Bhairava;
yet, at all times, one must avoid moving the image of Durgā or among the Mothers.
The ninefold divisions have been fully declared; each one [of these] is a Mother (mātṛ).
Among them, the goddess Mātṛkā is Cāmuṇḍā, the slayer of Ruru.
"Among them, who is the leading goddess?
Where is she? O twice-born one, whose movement must be directed by the Aghora-weapon?
Are they not the subduers of the terrible Kālakūṭa and Vajra-demons, or are they Rākṣasas?"
O child, the *damanī* is nine syllables, while the *bālavakṣarā* is ten syllables; these are prescribed for movement.
Now drink the milk born of your mother according to the proper time.
Having bathed [the deity] with water over which the mantra has been recited one hundred times, one should offer the bali-oblation.
Having offered [the offering] mixed with blood from garments and accompanied by wine, meat, and unformed [substances] in all directions, one should likewise cause Carcikā to move.
For when the mantra-practitioner, being possessed, moves the Śivā,
then one should know there is safety, as the king protects the earth.
O son of Viṣṇu,
having moved the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) from the south, one should establish it in the north;
it should always be worshipped, O child, until the completion of the temple.
When the moments [of the rite] have been completed, one should enter by means of the ritual of consecration (pratiṣṭhā).
Or, when the image has become worn out, one should move the pedestal.
Having offered the heart, there should then be the movement;
having fashioned a golden tail, the wise one should likewise fashion another Śiva.
O twice-born one, let them turn back from the calf-cord;
O Lord, having prepared fuel-sticks of milky trees along with pieces of wood from the hump of a bull, one should perform the cremation.
[With a monkey-rope, one should cast a mountain into the great waters and then settle another.]
O best of the twice-born, one should perform everything by relying on the ritual procedure for consecration.
O child, one should install the deities according to their respective ordinances with mantras arising from the complete ritual limbs; this is the procedure for the Mothers.

O twice-born one, those palaces of the Goddess that have been restored after falling into ruin—one should know that they are not to be grieved for, for their great lord has shaken off all sin. (118.015)
The restorers of ruined [temples] shall obtain merit four times that of the original builder;
therefore, a wise person should protect what is dilapidated with every effort.
O child, in whatever region an empty temple stands, one should know that there will be fear, famine, or thieves. (118.017)
Just as the embodied soul, having abandoned a worn-out body, takes refuge in another,
so too the deities abandon an aged temple and go elsewhere.
When that place becomes empty, piśācas and other such beings take up residence there, causing fear to men; they drive them out from that location and bring about terrible death.

O child, those people residing there became devoid of purity upon hearing that terrible sound; there is no doubt that even great beings, when afflicted by planets and cursed by enemies, go to their destruction.
Therefore, O child, one should restore it for the sake of worship; otherwise, one should install a deity or even a temple, whether it be old or new. ||118:021||
A wise person should act in such a way that worship may be performed constantly;
the great sage shall obtain the root merit through even a portion of the material substance.
The perpetrator shall incur a fine of more than one hundred [paṇas] without hesitation;
the king receives a sixth part, and the subjects and the kingdom are purified.
[The letter *ka* and *ga*: thus ends] the one hundred and eighteenth chapter, titled "The Restoration of Dilapidated Deities," in the *Śrīdevīpurāṇa*.
[In the first [part], the procedure for the restoration and repair of dilapidated [shrines]: *ka* and *ga*].

Chapter 121:
The One Hundred and Twenty-First Chapter.
Brahmā said:
O best of gods, I shall describe the supreme ritual procedure for the fire, which accomplishes all desires, according to its names, divisions, rites, and other details.
The formal consecration of the fire must be performed by those who know the meaning of all the scriptures,
who have mastered the Vāma, Dakṣiṇa, Siddhānta, Vedānta, and Gṛhya systems.
The maintenance of the sacred fire must be undertaken by those who know all forms of prosperity;
otherwise, obstacles will arise to wealth and longevity.
Whether one is constantly ill or unfortunate, or even honored by the whole world—my son, as long as one has not understood this, one remains ignorant; but having known it, one becomes wise. (121:004)
Therefore, for one who possesses many branches of knowledge, ritual action is considered necessary with every effort;
thus, the eightfold classification of fire-pits (kuṇḍa) in its three varieties has been fully explained by me to you.
The manifold varieties of fire are, in fact, merely figurative designations for a single one;
likewise, women, children, the elderly, and śūdras may perform the oblation every day.
Fools,
however, [perform it] in a monastery or even in a kitchen, but never in a sacrificial pit;
having preserved the fire by means of consecrated names and various designations.
Those who know the meaning of the Great Vidyā and desire its fruit should offer oblations;
for it is heard, O child, that in ancient times the son of Vasu [acted] without knowing this.
One who performs a sacrifice in a consecrated fire shall suffer the loss of his kingdom;
likewise, one who maintains no sacred fire shall soon meet with death.

[The fire-offerer (agni-hotr) has gone where... therefore, one who does not know [the truth] should not offer oblations into an unstable fire. I shall, however, proclaim that knowledge by which accomplishment is produced. ||121:010||
Bṛhaspati said:
"O father, I desire to hear the meritorious ritual for the fire-wheel and the installation of the deities; please explain it out of your grace."
Brahmā said:
"O child Madhusūdana, I am indeed in the quadrangular maṇḍala,
while Rudra, who is saluted by all the gods, is in the shape of a bow."
In a square mandala, Agni is the consumer of oblations;
in a half-moon, he is Anala; thus is the fire sacrifice established.
[In manuscript *ka*, ten verses beginning from this point are missing.
Among the twice-born, the teacher is immediately the deity;
in water, the color is the deity; and upon *darbha* grass, the great serpents are the deities.
The Great Goddess is in the *sruc* ladle, while the three-eyed God is in the *sruva* ladle;
the God, who is devoted to their union, is saluted by all the gods.
The *praṇītā* water is to be known as the Earth; the great Maruts are in the *svāhā* call.
Know that the Seasons are in the flowers, and the Great Ocean is in the vessels. (121.016)
Gāyatrī is situated in the center of the altar, Soma in the sprinkling water;
Maṇibhadra is in the fuel, while Śikhin has the thunderbolt as his weapon.
One should recognize Hotṛ in the cups and other vessels;
Rudra is the deity in the bellows, while Vāsava resides in the palm-leaf fan.
In the mantras, all the hosts [of deities] are again within the ashes, O Śaṅkara;
the world-protectors are in the corners, and all the gods are in the syllable *oṃ*.
The Mothers, however, receive their portion in the oblation; Pūtanā bestows sparks.
He who is the other, supreme deity abiding in the sun and other luminaries, is the one possessed of splendor.
The morning oblation for the gods, performed at half a watch, bestows prosperity; the midday oblation for humans brings about beloved things and the like.
In the afternoon it belongs to the ancestors (pitṛs), and at twilight it pertains to the planets and elemental spirits;
at night, for the purpose of destroying sins, it accomplishes divine perfections (divyasiddhi).
It should be offered at the half-watch, and at midnight it is destructive;
at the remaining times, O child, it bestows sons, and at sunrise it grants all desires.
The sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) fulfills all desires and bestows all attainments;
the deity presiding over the moment should be offered the first oblation at the commencement of the rite.
Otherwise, O Brahmin, the fire-oblation is always fruitless,
whether it be performed with vessels made of wood, clay, copper, silver, gold, or other such materials.
The increase of merit is tenfold through offerings, ablutions,
and meals [performed] with marks of deities, such as the trident, the lotus, the conch, the discus, and the fire.
The wise one should take ghee, milk, fat, and so forth, for the bathing of the Goddess with sacrificial substances empowered by the *vasordhārā* [stream of wealth]. 121:027.
This should be performed with material offerings, or otherwise according to the prescribed rule;
the deities, being nourished, will grant complete satisfaction as promised in the Vedas.
O child, I have thus described to you the fruit of the arms of the presiding deities of the gods when they are present among the lowly— a fruit that brings prosperity to all the worlds and the gods.
If the officiating priests are devoid of mantras, they become perpetually impure;
therefore, those who do not know the Vedas must not offer oblations into an unconsecrated fire.
The officiating priests who know the mantras cause the deities to swell with strength; but the priest who does not know them certainly does not gratify the gods.
When the two mantras are found as the Hotṛ priests, the attainment of all fruits arises for everyone from the oblation;
therefore, one who knows the ritual application of mantras bestows auspiciousness even at dawn.
Viṣṇu is the deity of the eastern fire, Hara is stationed to the south, and Brahmā is stationed to the west; these are the deities residing in the fires.
One should recognize Rudra in the brilliance and Carcikā in the flame;
the three long-lived ones and Lakṣmī are the deities there among the Brahmins.
Thus established is the *kriyāyuṣa* fire-sacrifice, as well as the three fires;
the three gods, the three times, and the three fires are consecrated within the sacrificial chamber. ||121:035||
The Gārhapatya, the Dakṣiṇāgni, and the Āhavanīya— these three,
O best of the twice-born, have arisen from one and the same source, though they possess many distinctions.
