Brahmā said: O Brahmin, in former times, during the Kṛta age, there was but one fire,
the embodiment of Rudra, eternally established as the splendor of the Great Soul.
In the Tretā age, the great Dakṣiṇeśa, being released for the sake of sacrifice, became the Gārhapatya fire; from that, the Tamas-born Havanīya fire arose.
From Havanīyā were born the highly powerful Bharata and others,
fifty-one in number by name, who are the ordainers of the moving and the unmoving.
O twice-born one, tell us indeed their names and their deeds in many ways; describe the lineages and castes of those seven groups according to their divisions.
Bharatī, Varā, Māṅgalyā, Vibhu, Bala, Aṅgiras, Samudbhava, Jaya, Rudra, Saṃyuga, Kālika, and Bhava. ||122:008||
In your supreme auspiciousness, there are those known as Vibhāva and Cala;
Sūrya, Jana, Śaśānka, the Viśvedevas, Parāvasu, Kalmāṣa, Saṃcaya, Ghora, Vaḍavāgni, and Varāntaka. ||122:009||
Jjala,
Dakṣa, Nidhīśvara, Kāma, Kālāntaka, Parāntaka, Bībhatso, Vijaya, Dhūmra, Kṛṣṇavarṇa, and Hāṭaka. ||122:010||
Ajita, Śaṅkara, Śaṅkha, Śuddhida, Jayada, Guru, Apara, Aparājita, Ka, Pratāpa, Bahuda, and Śubha. ||122:011||
The profound,
the forest-dweller, the all-pervading, the source of bliss, the fulfiller of desires, the destroyer of enemies, the auspicious one—
he, through the purificatory rites beginning with conception, becomes the granter of all desires.
In accordance with his possessions and likewise by virtue of the fire-oblation,
one who eats light food and remains pure is proclaimed a "constant offerer" (nityahotṛ).

Having performed the five rites in the sacrificial fire according to the form of the *avigraha* and likewise by the power of the *hotṛ*, one always attains success; for otherwise, the *caru* offering in the oblation would fail to bestow all accomplishments. (122.014)
For Agni resides in the *ādhāna* rite; he is established in the *puṃsavana*; in the *sīmantonnayana* he is named Maṅgala; and in the *jātakarman* he is remembered as Vibhu. (122:015)
Bala is declared for the naming ceremony; Aṅgiras is considered appropriate for the first feeding; Samudbhava and Vahni for the tonsure; and Jaya for the binding of the sacred vow.
Rudra, known as Godānika, is prescribed for marriage;
Agni, known as Kālika, is ordained for the Agnihotra sacrifice.
The fire existing in the household (āvasathya) should be known as belonging to the Viśvedevas;
the fire of the stomach (jaṭhara) is Vahni, and Kalmāṣa is the fire for the consumption of nectar (amṛtabhakṣaṇa).
The Sun is for the great oblation, Water is for the immersion in water;
the Moon is for the full-moon oblation, and at the time of destruction, Samvartaka is prescribed.
The *ghora* fire is abundant in wood; the *parānta* fire originates from bamboo; the *vaḍavāgni* is in the ocean; and the *dakṣa* fire is considered to be of the nature of digestion. (122:020)
Nidhīśa is in Vasudhārā, while Kāmadeva and Dhūmaja are in Tūṣaja; Kāmahā is in Agni, and Parāntaka is in Rathyā.
Bībhatsu, Kṣutkara, Vahni, Vijaya, and Nṛpagehaja;
Dhūmaja and Vṛkṣasamuttha—these are considered the black paths in the lamp.
Hema occurs in Tāpa; Vādya is born in Ajita and in the house of a mother;
Saṅgara is among the Mleccha peoples; and Śaṅkha indeed arises from the ripening of one's actions.
One should know purity in the Āditya [mandala], victory in the abode of Śukra,
the fire in the rite of initiation by the Guru, and another fire in the Tiṇḍila [sacrificial pits].
Know that the one born favorable to the throat has conquered the *lakṣahomas*;
Pratāpa is born from the blood of many gifts during the king’s consecration. (122.025)
For in the ritual of planetary invocation, Śubha is the fire produced from the fire-drill in the forest;
Vaidyuta is the all-pervading fire; and Śambhu is the fire arising from a gem. (122.026)
The Kāmika fire is for the practitioner; the Ripuhā fire is born of malevolent rites (abhicāra);
and the Śiva fire, which accomplishes all desires, is used for ten million oblations (koṭihoma). ||122:027||
O Brahmin, he who arises from the splendor of Śiva is celebrated as Kālāgni;
though he is one, he exists in many ways through his names and actions according to his state.
The fire has been described, my child; what more do you wish to ask?
Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-second chapter, titled "The Classification of Fires," in the glorious Devīpurāṇa.
[End of the first section on the classification of fires.]
Chapter 123:
The One Hundred and Twenty-Third Chapter.
Nṛpavāhana said:
O Brahmin, the fruit of the fire-rite has been told and understood;
now I wish to hear in truth about the specific qualities of the flowers and perfumes.
Agastya said:
O best of kings, just as it has been declared regarding vessels made of gold and silver,
so too is ghee superior for the fire-oblation, and sesame seeds for the smearing with unguents.
Sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, and onyx are considered the best for incense;
likewise, the quartet consisting of musk, camphor, saffron, and gorocana.
By anointing the Goddess with these, one shall obtain all desires:
*jātī*, *kaṅkola*, leaf, *elā*, *kuṣṭha*, saffron, and *patrikā*.
Jātīphala, latākhyā, snānagandhā, sadādharā, nāgakeśara, karpūra, surā, māṃsī, and bālaka. ||123:005||
O King, these massages are always declared to be dear to the Mother;
likewise, O King, the auspicious incense known as Nāgatu is eternally dear to the Goddess.
The ointment named Candra should be applied, which bestows all accomplishments;
as well as garlands of jewels and pearls, a canopy, and garments made of fine silk.
By always offering bells and the like, one shall obtain gold, flowers, and fruit;
or by offering flowers grown in the forest, or leaves produced on the mountains.
One should worship Śivā with flowers that have not been stale, which are free from holes, sprinkled with water, devoid of insects, and grown in one's own garden.

Merit becomes especially distinguished by the particular species of flower offered to a worthy recipient who is endowed with austerity, virtue, and good qualities, and who has reached the further shore of the Veda.
O best of kings, by giving ten pieces of gold to the flowers, one obtains that same fruit by giving it once to the Mothers.

Therefore, I shall describe the flowers and those fragrant leaves which are pleasing to the gods: the *ketakī*, the *atimukta*, the *baka*, the *bandhūka*, and the *bakula*—these are the [preferred] plants. (123:012)
The Kadamba, Karṇikāra, and Sindhuvāra lead to prosperity;
so too do the Punnāga, Campaka, Kunda, Yūthikā, and Navamallikā.
Damanaka, the lotus petal, and the hundredfold [flowers] increase merit;
likewise Tārā, arjuna, mallikā, bṛhatī, and śatapatrikā. (123.014)
The *karavīra*, *kusuma*, *kahlāra*, *bilva*, *pāṭala*, and *mālatī* flowers;
the *javā*, *vijola*, *aśoka*, and white and blue lotuses. 123:015.
The *paṅkaja* and the *śatapatra*—these ten [flowers] are for the increase of merit;
with these one should worship the Goddess, and she bestows swift accomplishment.
Drauṇapuṣpī, śamī, kṣīrī, nīlā, apāmārga, pattrikā, surasā, barbarā, bhadrā, surabhī, and karṇamallikā. ||123:017||
One should worship with Kadamba flowers at night; Mallikā flowers are equal for both times.
One should worship with divine and remaining flowers according to what is available.
One should discard flowers that are infested with insects or hair, those that are withered or stale, those that have fallen to the ground, and those that are otherwise damaged.
One should not worship the Goddess with unopened buds, nor should one offer fruit that is unripe.
One should carefully avoid fruit that is overcooked or perforated, even if it is ripe. (123.020)
If flowers are not available, one should offer even leaves;
if leaves are also unavailable, one should offer even fruits. ||123:021||
If even fruits are not obtained, then grasses, shrubs, and medicinal herbs [should be used];
and if even medicinal herbs are not obtained, she becomes honored through devotion alone.
For flowers offered individually, the fruit is ten gold pieces; for those same flowers when arranged together, the fruit is said to be double.
Whoever properly worships the Goddess with fragrant red flowers,
or even with garlands and beautiful blossoms, shall obtain infinite fruit.
Whoever worships the Liṅga even once with unbroken Bilva leaves,
being liberated from all sins, is glorified in the world of Śiva.

And whoever should establish a grove for Śiva, adorned with mango, *bilva*, and other trees, as well as with jasmine (*jātī*), *vijaya*, *parājā*, arka, oleander (*karavīra*), lotus (*abja*), and *kubjaka* flowers; ||123:026||
With *punnāga*, *nāga*, *bakula*, *aśoka*, *utpala*, and *campaka* trees,
as well as with plantains, *hempūṣpa*, and others— listen now to the fruit of his gift.
For as many thousands of years as there are leaves, flowers, seeds, and fruits [of that tree], so long does he rejoice in the world of the Goddess.
Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-third chapter, titled "The Ritual of Flowers," in the glorious Devīpurāṇa.

Chapter 124:
The One Hundred and Twenty-Fourth Chapter.
Nṛpavāhana said:
The exposition of all dharmas has issued forth from your mouth;
having heard it, I ask again concerning the worship of the Guru by the Goddess.
Agastya said:
[One should practice] in an underground chamber, or in the middle of a house, or in a cave in a mountain called Rakta,
or by a river, a stream, or the ocean, or in a courtyard free from wells.

O best of kings, having bathed according to the scriptural injunctions preceded by mantras in that auspicious site, which is filled with devoted people and situated upon a propitious foundation, [one should proceed].
Having placed the sixfold root-constellation upon the goddess who is well-proportioned and filled with water, he stands firm with his weapon;
when the weapon has been made of soft leather and filled with cotton and *tūla* fiber.
[He is] situated upon a similar seat; the mantra-practitioner stands thus, wearing well-perfumed garments, beneath a canopy and banners, adorned with fine cloths. ||124:005||

Having performed the rites of bathing and so forth for the Goddess in a delightful place according to the previously prescribed rule, using vessels made of gold, silver, or copper, [one should proceed].
The goddesses were separately perfumed with incense, accompanied by water-pots, scents, and other offerings; they were anointed with intoxicating unguents and draped in fine silk garments.
One should place necklaces made of pearls, ornaments of rubies,
and weapons such as swords, shields, nooses, and daggers.
One should present meat filled with ghee as an offering;
O child, one should worship the Supreme Goddess according to the previously mentioned procedure.
O child, having meditated upon the auspicious Goddess, who is both non-different from and superior to the physical form,
and having prostrated before that Goddess as well as before one's own self as being likewise [of that nature], [one should proceed].
Having performed various rites such as recitation for the sake of accomplishing the task,
one should then present the fire-rite (vahnikarma) that has been well-guarded.

The rite should be performed according to the previous injunctions in a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) protected by the *sruva* and *sruk* ladles and endowed with auspicious characteristics; therein one should establish the stream of wealth (*vasordhārā*).
The consecration, the vessels for the ritual juices, and the auspicious procedure for the fire-oblation (homa) have been described;
furthermore, the offering of bali should be presented in various dwellings.
[My *ka* and *ga*; I do not know the correct place of these notes.
To the auspicious world-protectors (*lokapāla*), the various yakṣas and vināyakas, to the worms, insects, and winged creatures, [I offer] the conceptualization of earth, water, and food. (124.014)
Having performed the imitation of water [libations], one should ask the Goddess for forgiveness; likewise, perform the worship of the Guru.
Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-fourth chapter, titled "The Procedure for Worship," in the Śrī Devīpurāṇa.
[In this first [part], the procedure for worship is concluded.
Chapter 125:
The One Hundred and Twenty-Fifth Chapter.
Agastya said:
The fruit of honoring the gods, fire, teachers, and sacred knowledge is equal;
such a teacher should be worshiped by them as the fulfiller of all desires.
He was a teacher of the distinctions among the sciences, the fires, and the deities; he spoke according to reality, followed the path of logic, and was a remover of doubts. ||125:002||
The words spoken by him are to be trusted by the wise regarding merit and sin as they truly are; failing to hear them, one goes downward.
Therefore, with every effort, one should fully worship the Guru as Śiva, for the sake of helping others and for one's own liberation. 125:004.
One should worship the Guru, the speaker of Śiva’s words, as one would Śiva himself;
his worship is prescribed according to the ritual procedure for the Goddess.
One should offer gifts such as gold, cows, jewels, land, and so forth. (125:005)
A house, a pavilion, knowledge, and so forth, as well as beds, staffs, and the like—whatever is most cherished on earth should be given especially to the guru. (125.006)
O best of kings, when he is satisfied, one obtains everything—
even if one is powerless or even separated from all sins.
In cases where the intentions of the preceptor are not manifest, one should consume his great wealth with devotion;
however, for one who is capable, there is no obstacle to the sacrifice, provided he does not inform the preceptor of it. (125.8)
Nevertheless, O lady rich in asceticism, the devotion of Vala, as well as that of Pārtha, Janamejaya at his sacrifice, and those of other great-souled ones, did not waver.
They become creators of obstacles, yet through one's fortitude, they become bestowers of boons upon them.
Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-fifth chapter, titled "The Ritual for the Worship of the Guru and the Deity," in the Śrī Devīpurāṇa.
[In the first incarnation of the Goddess, the ritual for the worship of the Guru.]
Chapter 126:
The One Hundred and Twenty-Sixth Chapter.
Nṛpavāhana said:
O dear one, I wish to hear in truth about those obstacles that arise for those engaged in the recitation and study [of the Vedas], and how they are to be pacified.
Agastya said: "O child, the remembrance of the Goddess is proclaimed in many ways as the destroyer of all obstacles; nevertheless, I shall describe it to you."
Through recitation, one attains purity of self; through the fire-ritual, prosperity;
and through prosperity, here in this world, both ritual actions and those that grant liberation are accomplished.
Therefore, having purified oneself through recitation and other practices, one should commence the fire-ritual;
for this, O son, is the basis of all accomplishments and the bestower of fruits in this world.
Then, in the fire named after the [deity] previously mentioned, within a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) possessing the characteristics described above,
he who is fully equipped with the ladle (śruva), the oblation materials, and so forth, [should proceed] for the sake of Agni.
First, the wise one should sprinkle the sacrificial pit with water consecrated by mantras;
thereafter, he should encircle it with the armor-mantra (kavaca) in the proper sequence.
O King, one should perform the re-scratching with the seed-syllable of the weapon:
three lines to the south, north, and west, as well as in the center and the north.
Then, the knower of the ritual procedure should perform sprinkling again with the *kavaca* mantra;
he should then once more install the extensive [deity] in the center of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) with the syllable *praṇava*.
Then, one should constantly place within that [the Śakti], which resembles a thousand lightning flashes, consists of sacrifice, and has large eyes, by means of the Yonimudrā.
[Bhānumatī is *ka*;
Ṛtumatī is *ga*.
He who destroys the union of the two Keśavas, remaining in the second stage of life (*dvitīyāśrama*).
The god has vanished within Keśava; this goddess is within the sacrificial fire.
Having honored [the deity] with perfumes and flowers and having offered it, one who knows the ritual procedure should then prepare the fire for the purpose of satiating the Goddess.
By that very [process], he is liberated and joined with the surrounding [element];
that very fire, known as "other," is the accomplisher of all goals.
Having brought the sacrificial fire into either a copper vessel or an earthen bowl,
one should sprinkle it with the Astra-mantra and then again apply the seed-syllable.
Thereafter, one should encircle it with the armor-mantra according to the prescribed rule;
having established it in the Śiva-kuṇḍa, one should cast it into the path of the womb.
Having thus whirled it around, one should worship the heart again with the mantra called *Kajaya*;
in this way, O King, the rite of conception (*garbhādhāna*) for Jātavedas is accomplished.
Having honored the goddess Jayā with a prostration of the head, one should then worship her.
Thus, the *puṃsavana* rite is performed; now hear concerning the *sīmantonnayana*.
One should first worship Ajitā, and thereafter worship the seed-syllable of Śiva;
thus the parting of the hair (sīmanta) for the fire is performed upon the altar.
Having worshipped with the Astra-mantra, one should recite the Aparājita mantra of the Goddess;
thus the birth-rite (jātakarman) is performed, and thereafter one should assign a name.
Having worshipped Vighneśa, one should then assign the armor (kavaca);
thereafter, the Fire-god, stationed within the sacrificial fire, should cause his name to be heard by the Goddess.
Neither non-goddesses nor goddesses ever accomplish their tasks;
for that reason, they shine when the work is performed before the gods, fire, water, and the sun.
The Śūdras are for the purpose of procreation; those called Abhayā are for the performance of duties; Aṅkuśā and others are for awakening; and she called Vīṇā is for all ritual acts.
Having thus consecrated the fire for the Śūdra with the mudrās and mantras in their proper sequence,
he should then perform the fire-oblation (homa) according to the ritual prescribed in the scriptures.

One should spread darbha grass upon the seed-syllable of the heart and cause the enclosing sticks (paridhis) to be placed with their tips pointing east and north; then one should worship the deities once again.
Beginning from the east, one should worship Brahmā, Śaṅkara, Viṣṇu, and Mantreśa, together with Gāyatrī, seated upon their respective seats in due order.
Having taken recourse to the south-eastern direction, one should cause the portion of clarified butter (ājyabhāga) to be offered;
having first performed the act of placing [the vessel] on the fire, one should afterwards perform the act of skimming and so forth.
Having plucked out a mere tip of a blade of darbha grass with the fingernail,
take hold of it with the thumb and ring finger and perform the sprinkling of clarified butter.
Then, during the ritual immersion, the officiant should properly purify the ghee placed before him with a tuft of darbha grass, while reciting the "Jvala" mantra as prescribed for the forest rite.
Then, one should touch it with water from outside the *nairājana* vessel. ||126:027ef||
Having grasped the *śruva* and *sruca* ladles on all sides within the fire of his majesty,
and having touched all the *kuśa* grasses— the tips, the middles, and those used for worldly rites— [he performed the oblation].
The knower of the ritual procedure should place the clarified butter and other substances on the right side and likewise on the left; then, with the *hṛdaya-mantra*, he should commence all the rites.
Then the practitioner should again cover the garments with the goddess-mantras in their proper sequence;
furthermore, the earthly one (the practitioner) should perform the reopening [of the door] with the seed-syllable of the weapon (astra-bīja).
Having provided atonement with a great weapon, one should examine the clarified butter;
then, one should divide it threefold for Śiva, Soma, and likewise for Agni. 126:031.
Then, having gratified the fire and offered the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) in due order,
one should then perform the arrangement of the seats as previously described.
Having worshipped the Great Goddess in due order with perfumes and flowers according to the previously stated procedure, one should then perform the fire-oblation (homa).

When there is abundant sacrificial material and pure wealth, and the fire has been well-kindled—when it is smokeless and its flames are licking upward—he who kindles it with the sacred fuel; ||| 126:034 ||
One should worship with milk oblations according to the ritual for the Conqueror of Death (Mṛtyuñjaya);
O child, when free from passion, one becomes esteemed by the goddesses.
[Regarding the substance, what and where?
Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-sixth chapter, titled "The Procedure for Homa," in the Śrī Devīpurāṇa.

Chapter 128:
The One Hundred and Twenty-Eighth Chapter.
Brahmā said:
This scripture, which accomplishes all goals, issued forth from the mouth of Brahmā;
it was also proclaimed by him, O tiger among kings, to Naravāhana.
Indra obtained it through the prescribed rite, and Agastya likewise attained it;
Śiva, however, taught it to Brahmā in its extent of one million verses.
Śiva spoke this to Brahmā, the son of Dakṣa and Prajāpati: "Ka" and "Ga" were obtained by Śakra of the world; the science was spoken by the Lord.
It contains the origin of the Ghoras, the slayings and other rites, and the supreme propitiation of the Goddess.
The origin of the terrible [deities] for the purpose of slaughter, as well as the application of ritual action and yoga, which accomplish the four aims of human life. ||128:003ef||
Whoever recites or hears this first incarnation of the Goddess shall be liberated from saṃsāra and attain the supreme state. ||128:004||
Having worshipped Śiva upon the lion-throne of knowledge in the center, adorned with cloth, flowers, and other offerings, one should listen to or recite what has been learned.
Or else, having fashioned a splendid golden staff-seat (*daṇḍāsana*), beautifully adorned with various jewels and covered with a golden cloth; 128.006.
It may be made of silver, copper, or bell-metal, fashioned according to the proportions of Brahmā; or it may be produced from the heartwood of trees, or derived from horn, bamboo, and the like.
It was adorned above and below with gems, gold, conch shells, crystal, and pearls, as they were available.
A gem carved with various designs and bound with thread-marks,
[placed] upon two-fold, double-measured [surfaces] resembling the full moon. ||128:009||
Variegated and inlaid with gold upon its pedestals, it is set upon legs of fine cloth, silk, and divine materials, and produced from variegated fabrics and the like. (128.010)
It should be pierced, colored with flowers, or provided with the tops of ramparts; it should be endowed with four moon-shaped ornaments and be very beautiful with five colors.
Adorned with the tinkling sounds of small bells, situated at the four corners,
with well-defined mountain-like rampart peaks of five colors.
[Varakopeteḥ ka ga] with all kinds of garments produced, and with dangling balls; ||128:012ef||
Having performed the invocation in this manner, one should place [the manuscript] upon a staff-seat (daṇḍakāsana);
having placed the great scripture known as the Devī upon it, one should worship it. ||128:013||
Having diligently performed the adornment with the offering of the gift of knowledge,
his hands scented with perfumes and the like, he sits upon a magnificent seat.
Having meditated upon the auspicious Parameśvara, the Lord of the Goddess, within this scripture through the ritual practice of the gift of knowledge (vidyādāna),
the Goddess of Gods herself remains with her husband, who is saluted by the gods. 128.015
Having gone with his own body to sacred fords, royal palaces,
houses, villages, and cities, he should cultivate the supreme Dharma.
Having meditated according to the prescribed rule upon the auspicious Śiva— the listener with a pleasant body— and having performed the profound meditation,
one should daily offer perfumes, flowers, and various provisions in every age.
Having worshipped and bowed down, they stood with palms joined in reverence; all were seated on low seats, tranquil, and following the order of seniority. ||128:018||

In accordance with the nature of things, those who wish to hear— both the listeners and the speaker— should be free from other distractions at the commencement and conclusion of the exposition of knowledge.
Having uttered the mantra of the Goddess known as Śivā for the sake of all accomplishments, each disciple in turn should bring incense, flowers, and other offerings one by one. 128.020.
For the sake of all virtuous people, the reciter (vācaka), even if he is a bestower of knowledge and mantras,
should offer his hand for the traditional rites and present three flowers.
Even those who have sipped water (ācānta) should perform worship upon their heads with those [offerings] at the beginning, middle, and end.
Having thus performed worship with both power and devotion, accompanied by a ritual gift (dakṣiṇā), ||128.022||
Whoever causes the recitation of the Goddess’s book to proceed, for the benefit of all sentient beings and for their own liberation, [shall attain success]. (128.023)
I shall describe the fruit of that merit for both the listeners and the reciter:
wealth, long life, progeny, fame, wisdom, intelligence, and beloved happiness.
Having attained this here, one shall obtain peace at the end of the body;
provided that one does not fail to worship the Great Knowledge and it is not situated in an improper location.

One who recites [the Veda] goes to hell; therefore, one should cause it to be recited after having consecrated it, and likewise having honored the speech in the presence of the gods, the fire, and the guru.
Furthermore, O Sage, it should be stated by one possessed of intelligence for the benefit of the stream of Dharma:
how the Dharma, once set in motion, causes one to abandon non-Dharma. ||128:027||
Out of greed or fear, this scripture of the Goddess, whose essence is Śiva, must not be spoken [unauthorizedly];
however, by reciting it, peace shall prevail in the world—this should be kept in mind day after day.
They may go for the sake of kuśa grass and flowers, and for the worship of Śiva and Umā;
then, having completed the scripture, they should perform a special worship.
A wise man [should offer] with devotion to the Goddess, to the teachers of the Vidyās, to the Śiva-yogins, to virgins, to Brahmins and kinsmen, and to others as well. (128.30)
One should provide food for all these people in every way: for the poor and the needy, for friends, for those of one's own family, for virtuous persons, and finally for one's servants.
One should give a sacrificial fee to the preceptor: an auspicious pair of cows, Śiva, a pair of garments, a ring, and a meal filled with ghee.
The previously mentioned fee should be given to the reciter;
for one who has not been mentioned, a fee equal to half that of the teacher should be given.
And the wise man should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) according to his ability to the remaining Śiva-yogins; thereafter, he should illuminate them with a hundred lamps and other such offerings.
A canopy and a banner should be offered; O Goddess, food should be given to the God.
Worship must be performed according to the mantras; it is not [proper] when devoid of ritual reverence.
One should offer all flowers, incense, and so forth to Śiva and the Goddess; there is no doubt that through hearing this, one attains knowledge, merit, and great peace. (128.036)
[By the water of merit, O Ka; from that, there shall be inexhaustible fruit, O Ka Ga.
Having thus performed the illumination of the Goddess and the scripture with devotion, the giver of the lamp of Śiva has his mass of darkness destroyed. ||128:037||
With the impurity of sin shaken off, you are purified; of this there is no doubt.
O Deva, all worlds indeed become divine realms when thus cultivated.
Listen to the fruit that one who is liberated from all sins without exception shall obtain:
having fearlessly uplifted his lineage, he shall be joined by his wife, sons, and others.
Accompanied by many affectionate kinsmen, servants, and dependents—
together with all these— he shall go to the glorious city of Śiva.
Mounted upon a great celestial chariot, endowed with all objects of desire,
he shall enjoy great pleasures there for as long as the moon and the sun endure.
By his own will, he is the giver, the taker, and the creator within the temple of Śiva, until the great dissolution;
then, at the end of the pralaya, having attained supreme knowledge and yoga.
Then, by the grace of the Goddess, one is liberated; there is no doubt in this matter.
Therefore, one should perform the recitation of the Goddess’s book as it has been understood.
By the grace of the Supreme Lord, through devotion to Śiva day by day, it bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
there is no pestilence, nor famine, nor demons, nor diseases.
The king who constantly listens to the Śiva-dharma does not die an untimely death, nor is he slain by weapons. (128.045)
In that highly meritorious region, O King, the Goddess is ever present;
having heard her even once as she speaks, O lord of men, through the application of the mind— (Note: The two verses are absent in manuscript Kha).
There, in the city of the devoted, Śiva sports together with Umā;
he grants all desires as well as fruits wished for by the mind.
O King, having heard this great merit once, one attains the status of a sacrificer;
in the winter, however, one goes to the world of Brahmā, and in the cool season, one dwells with Viṣṇu.
On that day of great merit, for that King Candramas,
having enjoyed all pleasures here with his retinue, [he shall attain the highest state].
In the excellent city before the Goddess, Śiva sports together with Vidyutā,
enjoying vast pleasures as long as the moon and stars endure.
[These two verses do not appear in manuscript *ka*] In the spring, the goddess Umā, the bestower of all happiness, is worshipped;
in the summer, the outer world is endowed with all desired objects.
Having enjoyed great pleasures in that Brahma-world, he is honored in the world of the gods;
during the rainy season, O King, the ruler hears of and goes to the world of Rudra.
O best of kings, one who hears this three times with devotion attains all desires and sovereignty; moreover, one is liberated from all sins. (128.053)
One's lineage shall become pure and bring forth the fruits of all desires;
having heard these five, the great meditator is glorified in the heavenly world.
Yama is constantly pleased with the community of mothers because they do not discriminate;
my speech would not be able to describe his enjoyment.
Having enjoyed auspiciousness in this world, and at its conclusion [having departed] from the world of Śiva,
he heard of the slaying of Khaṭvā and likewise the birth of Vināyaka.
O best of kings, having worshipped the Goddess according to the prescribed rite, one becomes free from disease, attains the world of the Mother, and sports there happily for a long time. (128.057)
One should cultivate serenity so that Śivā may become manifest;
one should maintain virtuous conduct, consume auspicious food, and remain free from all attachments.
By reciting even this much of the Purāṇa, one shall obtain all desires;
by reciting it a hundred times or even half that, one shall attain Śiva directly.
And this *Abhyudayapāda*, which bestows all perfections (*sarvasiddhi*), O child, has been declared by three hundred and twelve of the most excellent men. (128.60)
Oṃ, salutations to Durgā.
Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-eighth chapter, titled "The Procedure for Recitation," in the glorious Devīpurāṇa.
